Federal departments and agencies must cooperate with the board and give it information it needs, and the board is set to end one year after the order.

10108.s: This order sets up the United States Mission to the United Nations and says who is part of it, including representatives, deputies, staffs, and offices. It makes the U.S. Representative to the United Nations the Chief of Mission and gives that person responsibility for coordinating the Mission and managing its administration, including personnel and budget matters. It also says the Deputy Representative serves as Deputy Chief of Mission and acts as Chief of Mission when the Representative is absent.

10109.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate disputes between the Texas & Pacific Railway Company and its subsidiaries and certain of their employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. From the date of the order and for thirty days after the board reports, no change may be made in the conditions tied to the disputes except by agreement.

10107.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 8232 of September 5, 1939, which was about control of the Panama Canal and the Canal Zone. It affects that earlier order and ends it.

10106.s: This order creates a Board of Inquiry to look into a labor dispute between certain bituminous coal operators and their employees represented by the International Union, United Mine Workers of America. The dispute involves wages and terms and conditions of employment. The Board must report to the President and then continue to do any other work required under the law until the President ends it.

10105.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad Company and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. For thirty days after the board reports, the company and its employees may not change the conditions that led to the dispute unless they agree.

10104.s: This order defines certain military and naval installations, equipment, and official documents as needing protection against public spread of related information. It covers items marked "top secret," "secret," "confidential," or "restricted" at military, naval, or air-force locations, in certain airspace and naval harbor areas, and in some commercial work for the Army, Navy, or Air Force. It also replaces a previous executive order with the same subject.

10103.s: This order changes rules for certain civilian employees of the Executive branch who are transferred to public international organizations that the United States participates in. It says some transferred employees will be treated as being on leave from their federal jobs for up to three years while they work for the organization, if they are later reemployed by the Federal Government. It also restores and changes rules for certain war-service indefinite appointees, including when they can be treated as having competitive status and how some service time is counted.

10101.s: This order changes an earlier order about the Panama Canal and the Canal Zone. It says the organization for care, maintenance, sanitation, operation, and protection of the Panama Canal and the government of the Canal Zone will be called The Panama Canal. It also puts that organization under the Governor of the Panama Canal, with supervision by the Secretary of the Army, and creates a Lieutenant Governor role.

10102.s: This order transfers several buildings, docks, piers, coal-handling facilities, railroad roundhouses, car shops, oil-handling facilities, a printing plant, and gasoline service stations in the Canal Zone from The Panama Canal to the Panama Railroad Company. It also transfers related personnel, property, records, assets, contracts, obligations, and liabilities for those operations, with some exceptions listed in the order. One dock area stays owned by The Panama Canal but continues to be operated by the Panama Railroad Company, which must maintain and repair it. Most of the order takes effect on July 1, 1950, but section 5 and part of section 9 take effect on February 1, 1950.

10100.s: This order sets rules for allowances granted by the Director of Central Intelligence. In places where State Department regulations apply, those allowances must match the Secretary of State’s allowances; in other places, they should follow those general standards and rates as closely as practicable. The Director may also issue further regulations to carry out the order.

10098.s: This order changes a prior executive order about regulations for parts of the Career Compensation Act of 1949. It says that order takes effect on October 1, 1949, and stops being effective on March 31, 1950.

10097.s: This order designates and authorizes A. Cecil Snyder to perform the duties of Judge of the United States District Court for the District of Puerto Rico as Acting Judge. He may sign necessary papers and records without extra compensation when the judge is absent, ill, or otherwise legally disabled during 1950.

10096.s: This order sets a uniform patent policy for inventions made by Government employees. It says the Government will get the rights to some inventions made during work, with Government resources, or as part of official duties, and in some cases the employee keeps title while the Government gets a license for Government use. It also creates a Government Patents Board and gives the Chairman duties to help apply the policy and settle disputes.

10095.s: This order creates the President's Water Resources Policy Commission in the Executive Office of the President. The commission is to study federal responsibility for water resources and make recommendations on their development, use, and conservation, including related land uses and public purposes tied to water resources. It also directs federal departments and agencies to cooperate with the commission and provide information and assistance. The commission must submit its final report to the President by December 1, 1950.

10094.s: This order further exempts Clyde B. Aitchison from compulsory retirement for age. It lets him keep serving as a member of the Interstate Commerce Commission until his successor is appointed and has qualified.

10093.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 9512 from January 16, 1945. That earlier order dealt with coordination of the allocations of field positions subject to the Classification Act of 1923, as amended.

10092.s: This order sets aside airspace below 4,000 feet over parts of the Superior National Forest in Minnesota. After January 1, 1951, aircraft may not fly in this reserved airspace unless they follow the order and rules set by the Secretary of Agriculture. The order allows flights for emergency landings, safety, official business, rescue work, and some travel to and from private lands.

10091.s: This order extends the trust periods, or other limits on selling, for patents on Indian lands that would expire during 1950. The extension lasts 25 more years from the date the trust would otherwise end. It applies to tribal and individual Indian lands, except in cases where Congress kept the power to make the extension itself.

10090.s: This order makes certain corporation income tax returns open to inspection by the Federal Trade Commission. It covers returns for the calendar year 1949, fiscal years ending in 1949, and taxable years ending after June 30, 1949, and before July 1, 1950. The inspection must follow rules set by the Secretary of the Treasury.

10088.s: This order makes changes to the customs field organization. It designates Neah Bay, Washington, as a customs port of entry, revokes the port of entry designation for Guayanilla, Puerto Rico, changes the name of Sonoyta, Arizona, to "Lukeville, Arizona," and extends the Lawrence, Massachusetts, port of entry to include North Andover. These changes affect the customs ports of entry in Washington, Puerto Rico, Arizona, and Massachusetts.

10089.s: This order suspends compliance with certain statutory provisions about some kinds of employment in the Canal Zone. It does not change the provisions about how much compensation may be received by people in skilled, technical, clerical, administrative, executive, or supervisory jobs there. Those jobs include people employed directly or indirectly by the United States Government or by a corporation partly or wholly owned by the government.

10087.s: This order amends a prior order to transfer administration of certain World War II United States military cemeteries to the American Battle Monuments Commission. It moves related supplies, equipment, records, and some unused Army funds for those cemeteries. The transfer applies to the listed cemeteries and takes effect when the Army finishes its mission at each one, but no later than December 31, 1951.

10086.s: This order designates the South Pacific Commission as a public international organization. It makes the commission entitled to the privileges, exemptions, and immunities under the International Organizations Immunities Act. It also says this does not limit any privileges, exemptions, or immunities the commission may already have or later receive by treaty or congressional action.

10085.s: This order amends a previous executive order about allowances and allotments for government personnel on foreign duty. It covers civilian officers and employees of the Government and the rules for living-quarters, cost-of-living, and representation allowances. The amendment is effective as of August 24, 1949.

10084.s: This order adopts existing regulations and departmental rules, where they apply, as the regulations needed under Titles II, III, and V of the Career Compensation Act of 1949. It affects the administration of those parts of the law. The order takes effect on October 1, 1949, and stops being effective on January 31, 1950.

10083.s: This order revokes parts of three earlier executive orders that had given certain international organizations privileges, exemptions, and immunities under the International Organizations Immunities Act. It applies to the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, the Inter-American Coffee Board, and the Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees, which had ceased to exist or were being liquidated.

10082.s: This order sets up committees to help run the reciprocal trade-agreements program and to collect advice from government agencies and interested persons before trade deals are made. It requires studies and recommendations on imported and exported articles, and it provides a way to review proposed trade concessions and other trade agreement terms. It also directs the committees to keep track of trade agreements already in force and to report on their operation and effect.

10080.s: This order lets certain Federal employees without competitive status gain competitive civil service status if their agency head recommends them within one year. It applies to employees in active duty status who were appointed before March 16, 1942, have continuous creditable service since then, meet the required rating or merit test, and pass a noncompetitive examination. A separation for one year or less because of reduction in force will not stop them from qualifying.

10079.s: This order transfers the lands, buildings, improvements, and furnishings listed under Class Two of a 1931 order to the permanent control and jurisdiction of the Secretary of the Interior. The property is to be used in the administration of the government of the Virgin Islands. It says the property is no longer needed for naval use.

10081.s: This order says that if the Postmaster General is absent or sick, the highest-ranking listed officer who is able to serve will do the job. The listed officers are Assistant Postmaster General Vincent C. Burke, Paul Aiken, Joseph J. Lawler, and Walter Myers, and the order ends when a Deputy Postmaster General is appointed and qualified unless the President directs otherwise.

10077.s: This order transfers administration of the Island of Guam from the Secretary of the Navy to the Secretary of the Interior, effective July 1, 1950. It directs the Navy and Interior departments, along with other executive departments and agencies, to cooperate on the transfer. It also revokes the 1898 order that had placed Guam under the Department of the Navy.

10078.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Monongahela Connecting Railroad Company and certain of its employees. The employees are represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days, and for that period no change may be made, except by agreement, in the conditions that led to the dispute.

10076.s: This order makes certain income, excess-profits, and declared value excess-profits tax returns open for inspection by the Military Renegotiation Policy and Review Board. It applies to returns made under the Internal Revenue Code for 1939 and later years, subject to the conditions in the Treasury decision for that Board.

10075.s: This order removes certain public lands in and around the town site of Ford from Naval Petroleum Reserve No. 2 and sets them aside for townsite purposes. It says the oil and gas deposits in those lands will stay part of the reserve for the use and benefit of the United States Navy. The Secretary of the Interior is directed to dispose of the lands under the townsite laws.

10074.s: This order discontinues the district land office at Carson City, Nevada, and transfers its business and necessary archives to a new district land office in Reno, Nevada. It affects the work and records of that land office and takes effect at the close of business on August 12, 1949.

10073.s: This order exempts Eugene Black, a Judge of the Tax Court of the United States, from compulsory retirement for age. The exemption lasts for an indefinite period, but not beyond the end of his present term of office.

10072.s: This order directs department and agency heads to review their programs for better economy and effectiveness, make regular checks of operations, and report progress to the Bureau of the Budget. It also tells the Bureau to review agency plans, help agencies improve their operations, and report to the President. The order creates an Advisory Committee on Management Improvement to help the President with government-wide management improvement efforts.

10070.s: This order changes the travel rules for claimants and beneficiaries of the Veterans' Administration. It lets the Administrator of Veterans' Affairs approve a mileage allowance of 5 cents a mile instead of actual travel expenses, including lodging and subsistence, for travel under prior authorization to or from a Veterans' Administration facility or other place for vocational rehabilitation, examination, treatment, or care. It also allows payment to the person or organization that paid those travel expenses. The order became effective on August 1, 1949.

10069.s: This order changes rules for paying travel and transportation costs when civilian federal employees are transferred to a new official station for permanent duty. It says the employee’s travel expenses and the transportation of the immediate family must follow the Travel Expense Act of 1949 and the Standardized Government Travel Regulations. It also allows advances of funds for moving household goods and personal effects within the continental United States, with required written details and limits on how the amount is figured.

10068.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 2458 from September 20, 1916. That earlier order had established an inter-departmental board on international service of ice observation, ice patrol, and ocean derelict destruction.

10071.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Southern Pacific Company (Pacific Lines) and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days, and the company and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement during that time and for thirty days after the report.

10067.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Missouri Pacific Railroad Company and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees cannot change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

10065.s: This order ends the Office of Defense Transportation and the office of its director. It assigns the Interstate Commerce Commission to finish liquidating the office’s affairs and transfers its remaining records, property, personnel, funds, and some functions to that commission. The order also lets the commission act under the title "Administrator of the Affairs of Federal Managers" for this work.

10064.s: This order extends a suspension of the eight-hour law for laborers and mechanics working for the Departments of the Army and the Air Force on certain public works. It applies when the Secretary of the Army or the Secretary of the Air Force finds the suspension essential to the supply and maintenance of military or naval forces, essential construction, or international commitments. The order also says these workers' wages are to be figured on an eight-hour day rate, with overtime paid at time and one-half for hours over eight in a day. It takes effect on July 1, 1949, and extends the suspension to July 1, 1950.

10066.s: This order adds certain lands in Polk County, Tennessee, to the Cherokee National Forest. The lands are transferred under an agreement between the Tennessee Valley Authority and the Department of Agriculture. It also includes a five-room stucco building known as Parksville Village Building #26.

10062.s: This order creates the position of United States High Commissioner for Germany as the Chief of Mission. The High Commissioner becomes the top United States authority in Germany and can carry out United States government functions there, except commanding troops, under the supervision of the Secretary of State and the direction of the President. The order also keeps the United States commander in Germany under the Joint Chiefs of Staff for military matters.

10061.s: This order changes the rules for travel and living allowances for enlisted men in the Army, Air Force, Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard, and for members of the Coast and Geodetic Survey and Public Health Service on duty outside the continental United States or in Alaska. It sets new daily allowances for travel when quarters or meals are not provided. It also says the revised rules will stay in effect during the fiscal year ending June 30, 1950, unless they are changed or revoked sooner.

10060.s: This order returns the land known as the Keaahala Military Reservation in Kaneohe, Oahu, to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. It also cancels the reversion, reservations, and restrictions in earlier executive orders for that land.

10058.s: This order restores a parcel of government land at Keaukaha, Waiakea, South Hilo, Hawaii, to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. The land, together with any improvements on it, had been set aside for use by the Navy Department for military purposes but was no longer needed for that use.

10059.s: This order changes rules for aerial flights by members of the reserve components of the armed services who are not in active military service and are in inactive-duty-training pay status or drill pay status. It sets flight and time requirements for one, two, or three calendar months, and says the flights may be made during drills, training, instruction, or other duty times. It also changes the title and preamble language from "National Guard" to "reserve components of the armed services."

10057.s: This order transfers administration of certain World War II U.S. military cemeteries in Europe, Tunisia, and the Philippine Islands from the Department of the Army to the American Battle Monuments Commission. It also transfers related supplies, equipment, facilities, records, and some unexpended funds for these functions. The Department of the Army may return to the cemeteries later to make exhumations or reinterments if needed.

10056.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Union Railroad Company (Pittsburgh) and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report is made, the company and its employees may not make changes in the conditions that led to the dispute unless they agree to do so.

10055.s: This order changes an earlier rule that limited Federal officers and employees from holding local offices. It allows Federal officers and employees who live in the City of Norris, Tennessee, to be candidates for and hold local municipal offices if their agency approves. The agency must decide that the local office will not interfere with their Federal duties.

10053.s: This order approves regulations for moving household goods for members of the Air Force, Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, Coast and Geodetic Survey, and Public Health Service. The rules cover packing, crating, shipping, drayage, hauling, storage, and claims for household goods. They also set weight limits and say members must pay extra costs for unauthorized items or weight over the allowed limit.

10054.s: This order changes a prior rule on reemployment rights for U.S. personnel transferred to public international organizations. It gives Gerald C. Gross, a former Federal Communications Commission employee now with the International Telecommunication Union, until five years after he began service there to be terminated without prejudice, if he meets the other requirements in the order.

10050.s: The order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Railway Express Agency, Inc. and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report is made, neither side may change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

10051.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Aliquippa and Southern Railroad Company and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report is made, no change in the conditions that led to the dispute may be made except by agreement.

10048.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Southern Pacific Company (Pacific Lines) and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Enginemen. The board must report its findings to the President within 30 days. During that time, and for 30 days after the report, the company and its employees may not change the conditions that led to the dispute except by agreement.

10049.s: This order gives the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of the Treasury the power to set the clothing and cash allowances for enlisted men in the armed forces and the Coast Guard. It covers the Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Naval Reserve, Marine Corps Reserve, Coast Guard, and Coast Guard Reserve. Existing rules stay in effect until they are changed, revoked, or replaced under this order.

10046.s: The order transfers jurisdiction over certain lands, waters, water rights, improvements, and structures from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of the Interior in several listed areas. It says those lands will be administered under the Taylor Grazing Act. It also withdraws other public lands in listed areas from most public land laws and reserves them for use by the Department of Agriculture under the Bankhead-Jones Farm Tenant Act.

10045.s: The order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Wabash Railroad Company, the Ann Arbor Railroad Company, and certain of their employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the companies and their employees may not change the disputed working conditions except by agreement.

10043.s: This order changes the name of the President's Committee on Religious and Moral Welfare and Character Guidance in the Armed Forces. It also amends the earlier executive order that created the committee.

10044.s: This order changes an earlier rule that barred most federal officers and employees from holding state or local offices. It lets employees of the United States Atomic Energy Commission hold offices such as constable, deputy sheriff, or other law enforcement officer, and also hold state or local offices in the states where they are on duty. The General Manager or a designee must approve each case and decide that the office will not interfere with their Commission duties.

10041.s: This order returns certain lands in Hanapepe, Kona, Kauai, and the improvements on them to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. The lands had been reserved for use by the Navy Department as a radio station, but they are no longer needed for that use. The lands include Lots 1, 2, and 3 of Hanapepe Beach Lots and the land between those lots and the highwater mark.

10042.s: The order changes customs field organizations in several places. It designates new customs ports of entry in Elkin, North Carolina, and Cordova, Alaska, and revokes the port designations for Cheboygan, Michigan, Arecibo, Puerto Rico, and Arroyo, Puerto Rico. It also extends the limits of the customs ports of entry in Alexandria Bay, New York; Wilmington, North Carolina; Mobile, Alabama; and San Francisco-Oakland, California.

10040.s: This order changes a prior executive order about certain employment rules in the Canal Zone. It says the suspension of those rules does not change the provisions on how much pay may be received by people in skilled, technical, clerical, administrative, executive, or supervisory jobs there. The covered jobs are those employed directly or indirectly by a branch of the United States Government or by a company or corporation partly or wholly owned by the United States Government.

10039.s: This order authorizes the Civil Service Commission to confer a competitive status on Miss Winifred R. Donnellon, an employee of the United States Passport Agency in the Department of State. It allows this to be done without following the usual competitive Civil Service Rules. The order says she has served in the Department of State for many years under appointments excepted from civil-service requirements.

10038.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the carriers named in the order and certain of their employees. The board is to report its findings to the President within thirty days. From the date of the order and for thirty days after the board reports, the carriers and their employees may not make changes in the conditions out of which the dispute arose except by agreement.

10036.s: This order opens 1,240 acres in the Angeles National Forest in California to location and entry under the mining laws of the United States. It applies subject to valid existing rights and existing withdrawals, and the change takes effect 35 days after the order is signed.

10035.s: This order designates Luis Negron-Fernandez to serve as Acting Judge of the District Court of the United States for Puerto Rico during 1949. He may handle the judge’s duties and sign papers and records when the judge is absent, ill, or otherwise legally unable to serve. He will do this without extra compensation.

10037.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate a dispute between the Denver & Rio Grande Western Railroad Company and certain of its employees represented by the Switchmen's Union of North America. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days, and the railroad and its employees may not make changes in the disputed working conditions except by agreement during that period and for thirty days after the report.

10033.s: This order sets rules for how the federal government gives statistical information to intergovernmental organizations it belongs to. It gives the Director of the Bureau of the Budget and the Secretary of State roles in deciding what information is provided and which federal agencies prepare and transmit it. For requests from the International Monetary Fund or the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the National Advisory Council decides what information is essential, and certain agencies may be required to collect or provide it. The order does not allow information to be shared if it is withheld for military security or must be kept confidential by law.

10034.s: This order further exempts John Monroe Johnson, a member of the Interstate Commerce Commission, from compulsory retirement for age. The exemption lasts for an indefinite time, but not beyond the end of a further term of office as a member of the commission. For this order, that term ends when his successor is appointed and qualified.

10031.s: This executive order adds a rule for commissioned officers of the Public Health Service about separation on grounds of disloyalty. It says their loyalty to the Government of the United States may be investigated, reviewed, and determined under the loyalty program rules in Executive Order 9835. If the Administrator finds reasonable grounds to believe an officer is disloyal, that officer must be separated from the Service.

10032.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Akron, Canton & Youngstown Railroad Company, other listed carriers, and certain employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. From the date of the order and for thirty days after the report, the carriers and their employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

10030.s: This order gives the Secretary of Defense authority to supervise and control the administration of the District of Columbia National Guard for the President. That authority does not apply when the Guard is in active Federal service or on active emergency duty in the District of Columbia. The Secretary of Defense must also submit recommendations to the President about appointing the Commanding General and the Adjutant General.

10028.s: This order sets definitions for “noncombatant service” and “noncombatant training” under the Selective Service Act of 1948. It says noncombatant service includes unarmed units, service in the medical department, and some other assignments that do not require the use of arms in combat. It also says noncombatant training is training that does not involve the study, use, or handling of arms or weapons.

10029.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate a dispute between Northwest Airlines and certain of its employees represented by the International Association of Machinists. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report is made, Northwest Airlines and its employees may not change the conditions that led to the dispute except by agreement.

10027.s: This order extends the trust periods, or other restrictions on sale, for patents applying to Indian lands that would expire during 1949. The extension lasts 25 more years from the date the trust would otherwise end. It applies to tribal and individual Indian lands, except where Congress has specifically kept the authority to extend the trust period for itself.

10026.s: This order adopts the 1949 Manual for Courts-Martial, U.S. Army, for use in the Department of the Air Force. It applies the manual and a prefatory set of changes to Air Force personnel and to some Army personnel under Air Force command. It also keeps some earlier cases going under the 1928 manual and sets rules for acts, punishments, and court-martial service during the transition period.

10025.s: This order designates the World Health Organization and the Caribbean Commission as public international organizations under the International Organizations Immunities Act. It gives them the privileges, exemptions, and immunities covered by that law. It also says this does not reduce any other privileges, exemptions, or immunities they may have from treaty or congressional action.

10024.s: This order opens the listed land in California to location and entry under the mining laws of the United States. It applies to the described 320 acres, subject to valid existing rights and existing withdrawals.

10022.s: This order transfers the use, possession, and control of the Chattanooga Boat Yard in Tennessee, along with the buildings and other improvements there, from the Department of the Army to the Tennessee Valley Authority. The transfer includes the listed land and is subject to easements for the Belt Railway Company of Chattanooga, Tennessee.

10021.s: This order keeps Harry B. Mitchell, a member of the United States Civil Service Commission, exempt from compulsory retirement for age. It extends that exemption for an indefinite period of time.

10023.s: This order amends a prior order on clothing allowances for enlisted Navy and Coast Guard personnel. It adds a cash allowance of up to $80 for enlisted men, including chief petty officers, who serve with the United States Navy Band so they can buy the full dress uniform required for the band. The allowance applies to certain members now serving, later assigned, or later reenlisted or recalled to active duty, and it can be paid only once during any period of continuous active duty.

10020.s: This order prescribes a new Manual for Courts-Martial, U.S. Army, 1949. It applies to court-martial processes in the Army of the United States on and after February 1, 1949. It also says earlier investigations, trials already begun, and other actions begun before that date may continue under the 1928 manual, and it does not make punishable acts that were not punishable when done.

10019.s: This order closes several federal offices in the metropolitan area of the District of Columbia for one-half day on December 24, 1948. It also excuses federal employees in that area and in the field service from duty for one-half day, except for those excluded for special public reasons or where leaving duty would conflict with existing law.

10018.s: This order transfers control of certain tracts of land in Puerto Rico from the Secretary of the Interior to the Secretary of Agriculture. The land is to be administered for forest purposes, subject to valid existing rights. It covers described parcels in the municipalities of Luquillo and Rio Piedras.

10017.s: This order changes the rules for appointing postmasters of the fourth class. It raises the pay limit from $1,000 to $1,300 a year for appointments made on the basis of a post office inspector’s investigation and report. It also replaces a previous executive order on the same subject.

10016.s: This order sets the official coat of arms, seal, and flag for the Vice President of the United States. It describes their colors, symbols, and how they should appear, and says they are to be used only to represent the Vice President. It also revokes an earlier order that set the Vice President’s official flag.

10015.s: This order amends a prior order that created an emergency board to investigate disputes between the Akron & Barberton Belt Railroad Company, other carriers, and certain employees. It adds several rail carriers to the list covered by that order. It also changes the names of two railway labor organizations listed in the order.

10014.s: This order directs federal departments, agencies, and independent establishments to work with state and local authorities on water pollution control. It says they should take practicable steps to dispose of sewage, garbage, refuse, and other wastes from federal activities, and other products destroyed by federal regulatory authorities, in a way that follows state water protection programs. It applies to federal agencies and to state and local authorities involved in controlling water pollution.

10012.s: This order excludes certain positions filled by patients in hospitals operated by the Federal Government or the municipal government of the District of Columbia from the Classification Act of 1923, as amended. It says the pay for those positions will be set by department heads or the Commissioners of the District of Columbia, unless another law provides otherwise. The pay for each position cannot be higher than it would have been under the Classification Act.

10013.s: This order makes government policy to encourage the religious, moral, and recreational welfare and character guidance of people in the armed forces. It creates a President’s committee to study ways to carry out that policy, advise the Secretary of Defense and the military departments, and make recommendations to them and the President. Government agencies are asked to cooperate with the committee and provide information it needs.

10011.s: This order gives the Secretary of State authority to carry out certain presidential powers about allowances and rules for government personnel serving in foreign countries. It covers living-quarters allowances, cost-of-living allowances, representation allowances, and how those payments are accounted for. Existing rules stay in effect until they are replaced, and two earlier executive orders are revoked.

10009.s: This order revokes parts of two earlier orders that had barred certain Japanese or Korean citizens or subjects from entering the continental United States. It applies to those who entered the Territory of Hawaii under the passports described in the order and are now barred from legally entering or staying in the continental United States. It also directs the Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization, with the Attorney General's approval, to issue rules needed to carry it out.

10008.s: This order changes Selective Service rules for registration, classification, and medical examinations. It requires certain male persons who enter the United States after their age group’s registration date to register within 6 months, and it says certain male aliens who have not declared an intent to become citizens do not have to register if they fit listed categories. It also changes how local boards handle medical interviews, physical examinations, transfers, and records for registrants.

10010.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate disputes between the Akron & Barberton Belt Railroad Company, other named carriers, and certain employees represented by railway labor organizations. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. From the date of the order and for thirty days after the report, the carriers and their employees may not change the conditions out of which the disputes arose except by agreement.

10007.s: This order directs the Secretary of Defense and military department heads to organize all reserve component units and train additional active reserve members as needed for national security. It also calls for instruction and training programs for the reserve components, including the National Guard. The Secretary of Defense must report to the President within 60 days, and citizens and reserve members are urged to help build strong reserve forces.

10006.s: This order sets rules for how proposed executive orders and proclamations must be prepared, reviewed, signed, filed, numbered, and published. It requires them to be sent through the Bureau of the Budget, the Attorney General, and the Division of the Federal Register before they go to the President. It applies to executive orders and proclamations, but not to treaties, conventions, protocols, or other international agreements, or proclamations of them. It became effective when published in the Federal Register and replaced a 1936 executive order.

10005.s: This order creates the President's Advisory Commission on the Relation of Federal Laws to Puerto Rico. The commission is to advise the President on whether Puerto Rico should be exempted from some federal laws because of local conditions, and it may hold hearings and examine those laws. Federal departments and agencies are directed to cooperate with the commission and provide information it needs.

10004.s: This order sets up committees to help the President handle trade agreements and to gather advice and public views before any agreement is made. It requires notice, Tariff Commission review, and studies of imported and exported articles before recommendations are sent to the President. It also says the committees and the Tariff Commission must keep track of trade agreements already in force and report on them. It revokes earlier executive orders on the same subject.

10003.s: The order names the Displaced Persons Commission to make the investigations and written reports required under the Displaced Persons Act of 1948. Those reports must cover the character, history, and eligibility of displaced persons seeking admission into the United States. The Department of State, the Department of the Army, and other government agencies may be asked to help the Commission.

10001.s: This order sets rules for Selective Service medical interviews and armed forces physical examinations. It tells local boards when to call registrants in, how to review possible disqualifying physical or mental conditions, and when to cancel or issue further orders. It also lets some registrants ask to be transferred for a medical interview or physical examination if reporting to their own local board would be a hardship.

10000.s: This order sets rules for extra pay for some federal employees working outside the continental United States and in Alaska, Hawaii, and other U.S. territories. It lets the Secretary of State and the Civil Service Commission set places and rates for different types of extra compensation based on environment, hardship, unhealthful conditions, or higher living costs. It also says when employees may get these payments, how they are paid, and when they are not allowed for people serving under contract.

9999.s: This order suspends certain rules about employment in the Canal Zone during the present national emergency. It also suspends, for fiscal year 1949, rules that required citizens of the Republic of Panama or the United States to be employed in skilled, technical, clerical, administrative, executive, or supervisory jobs. The order says this action was taken because of a shortage of housing.

9998.s: This order sets rules for which U.S. officers and representatives have priority at diplomatic missions, ceremonies, receptions, international conferences, and in consular districts. It gives specific precedence among chiefs of mission, foreign service officers, military and other attachés, and certain consular and medical officers. It also says these rules replace two earlier executive orders.

9997.s: This order amends the travel and transportation payment rules in Executive Order No. 9805. It applies to civilian officers and employees of the United States who are transferred from one official station to another for permanent duty. The change takes effect for travel orders issued on or after July 1, 1948.

9995.s: This order restores certain parcels of land from the Schofield Barracks Military Reservation and the Wheeler Field Military Reservation on the Island of Oahu to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. The land is to be used for road purposes. It affects the specific parcels described in the order and is subject to the stated terms and conditions.

9996.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Public Belt Railroad Commission for the City of New Orleans and certain employees represented by two railroad labor organizations. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the railroad commission and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9994.s: This order changes the rules for Federal civilian employees who transferred to public or private agencies for national-defense or war work. It says their existing reemployment rights to Federal positions expire on October 22, 1948 unless they apply before then. It also keeps those rights for some people serving in a Federal agency being liquidated, or for some people leaving the armed forces or merchant marine, with limits on later actions that extend their service.

9993.s: This order sets regulations for commissioned officers and employees of the Public Health Service. It covers how officers are appointed, promoted, separated, retired, trained, paid, and disciplined. It also sets rules for leave, uniforms, titles, and boards that review medical and disciplinary matters.

9992.s: This order amends Selective Service regulations. It lets Selective Service officers buy printing and supplies, and it adds rules for when a registrant may get a permit to leave the United States. It says certain male aliens who have not declared an intention to become a citizen are not required to register and are relieved from liability for training and service, but they must carry an official document. It also adds and revises rules for placing certain aliens in Class IV-C.

9990.s: This order adds a Treasury Department representative to the Air Coordinating Committee. The Secretary of the Treasury will designate that representative, and the committee rules will apply to the Treasury Department the same way they apply to the other participating agencies.

9991.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate a dispute between the Pittsburgh & West Virginia Railway Company and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9988.s: This order sets out parts of the Selective Service Regulations under the Selective Service Act of 1948. It covers how local boards send classification questionnaires, handle conscientious objector and deferment claims, correct incomplete forms, get information from agencies, and use subpoenas. It also sets rules for classifying male registrants into the five main classes, including available, deferred, exempt, and over-age categories.

9989.s: This order gives the Attorney General control over certain foreign property and interests that are still blocked on September 30, 1948. It lets the Attorney General act on those assets and use powers under the Trading With the Enemy Act. Treasury orders and licenses for those assets stay in effect unless the Attorney General changes them.

9987.s: This order creates a Board of Inquiry to look into certain labor disputes in the maritime industry. The disputes involve steamship companies, contracting stevedores, contracting marine carpenters, and other related employers, along with employees represented by the International Longshoremen's Association. The Board is to report to the President and then continue to carry out other duties under the law until the President ends it.

9984.s: This order sets rules for clothing and cash clothing allowances for enlisted personnel in the Navy, Coast Guard, Naval Reserve, and Coast Guard Reserve. It also sets rules for a quarterly maintenance allowance for certain enlisted men and leaves other groups out, including some reservists and men holding temporary warrant or commissioned rank. The order replaces earlier executive orders and is effective for the listed fiscal year.

9986.s: This order says Navy vessels that have been stricken from the Navy Register and are not covered by other law may be sold at public sale to the highest acceptable bidder. They must be advertised for sale for at least thirty days, and the sale can be made regardless of appraised value. It also replaces Executive Order No. 9641 from October 15, 1945.

9981.s: This order sets a policy of equal treatment and opportunity for all people in the armed services, without regard to race, color, religion, or national origin. It creates an advisory committee of seven members to review armed services rules, procedures, and practices and to make recommendations to the President and defense leaders. Federal departments and agencies are directed to cooperate with the committee and provide information and services it needs.

9982.s: This order extends and keeps in effect rules for granting and accounting for certain foreign service allowances and allotments. It applies to those foreign service allowances and allotments through June 30, 1949.

9979.s: This order sets rules and definitions for the Selective Service Regulations under the Selective Service Act of 1948. It gives the Director of Selective Service authority to make rules, issue orders, appoint staff, spend funds, and carry out other duties under the law. It also sets requirements for Selective Service personnel, appeal boards, local boards, and advisors to registrants.

9980.s: This order requires federal personnel actions to be based on merit and fitness, with no discrimination because of race, color, religion, or national origin. It makes the head of each executive department responsible for carrying out fair employment policies and for naming a Fair Employment Officer. It also sets up a Fair Employment Board in the Civil Service Commission to review appeals, make recommendations, and coordinate fair-employment policies across departments.

9978.s: This order closes the district land offices at Blackfoot and Coeur d'Alene, Idaho. It transfers their business and necessary archives to a new district land office in Boise, Idaho.

9977.s: This order discontinues several district land offices in Oregon, South Dakota, and North Dakota. It moves the business and necessary archives from those offices to a new district land office in Portland, Oregon, or to the Bureau of Land Management in Washington, D.C. The order took effect at the close of business on July 30, 1948.

9976.s: This order amends a prior rule on allowances for quarters, subsistence, and per diem for enlisted members of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, and certain other services on duty outside the continental United States or in Alaska. It adds the Air Force wherever Army is named in that order and its title. It also raises the daily subsistence allowance when government messing facilities are furnished to $1.50 instead of $1.20.

9975.s: This order lets the Veterans' Administration pay travel expenses, including lodging and subsistence, for claimants and beneficiaries traveling with prior approval to or from a Veterans' Administration facility or other place for vocational rehabilitation, examination, treatment, or care. It also allows a mileage payment instead of actual expenses, and it can cover an attendant when one is needed. The Administrator may set rules to carry out the order, and this order replaces a 1944 executive order on the same subject.

9973.s: This order amends a civil service rule about certain federal jobs in Schedule A or B, and jobs excepted from the competitive service by statute. It says a person with competitive status in those positions is not protected against separation, unless the position has been designated as not mainly confidential or policy-determining. In those designated positions, a person with competitive status can be separated only under the Civil Service Rules and Regulations.

9972.s: This order designates the International Joint Commission between the United States and Canada as a public international organization under the International Organizations Immunities Act. That gives the organization the privileges, exemptions, and immunities covered by that law. It says this does not reduce any other privileges, exemptions, or immunities the organization may already have or may later get by treaty or congressional action.

9974.s: This order extends a suspension of the eight-hour law for laborers and mechanics employed by the Departments of the Army and the Air Force on certain public works. The suspension applies when the Secretary of the Army or the Secretary of the Air Force finds it essential for the supply and maintenance of military or naval forces, the completion of essential construction, or the fulfillment of international commitments. It extends the prior order until July 1, 1949, and the wages of these workers are to be figured on an eight-hour basic day with overtime paid at time and one-half for hours over eight in a day.

9970.s: This order creates a Board of Inquiry to look into a labor dispute in the bituminous coal industry. The dispute is between coal operators and employees represented by the International Union, United Mine Workers of America, and it involves wages and terms and conditions of employment. The Board must report to the President and then continue to do any other duties required under the law until the President ends it.

9971.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate disputes between certain railroad carriers under Federal management and workers represented by the national Maritime Union of America. The disputes involve the Grand Trunk Western Railroad Company, Chesapeake & Ohio Railway Company, Wabash Railroad Company, and Ann Arbor Railroad Company. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days, and the order says it does not reduce the Secretary of the Army's authority under Executive Order No. 9957.

9969.s: This order suspends the eight-hour-per-day limit for laborers and mechanics working for the Alaska Railroad on public work in Alaska. It applies for five months and only where the Secretary of the Interior finds the extra hours are needed to carry out the order. It also says these workers must be paid on a 40-hour workweek, with overtime at time and one-half for hours over 40 in a week.

9967.s: This order sets the line of succession for the Secretary of Agriculture if both the Secretary and the Under Secretary are absent, sick, resign, or die. It says the Assistant Secretary of Agriculture would act first, followed by the Administrator of the Rural Electrification Administration, the Governor of the Farm Credit Administration, and the Administrator of the Farmers Home Administration. It also replaces Executive Order No. 7465 from 1936.

9968.s: This order says that Assistant Secretaries of Labor may perform the duties of the Secretary of Labor if both the Secretary and Under Secretary are absent, sick, resign, or die. It also says the Solicitor of Labor may perform those duties if the Secretary, Under Secretary, and Assistant Secretaries are all absent, sick, resign, or die.

9964.s: This order creates a Board of Inquiry to look into certain labor disputes in the maritime industry. The disputes involve employers or ship owners and their employees on the Pacific Coast, the East and Gulf Coasts, and the Great Lakes and connecting waters. The board is directed to report to the President and may continue to do other duties allowed under the law until the President ends it.

9962.s: This order directs federal departments, independent establishments, and corporations to pay salaries and compensation to covered employees working outside the continental United States or in Alaska under the regulations and practices they used before April 20, 1948, until general regulations are issued. It also says those pay rates cannot be more than 25 percent above the rates for the same or similar work in the continental United States. No salary or compensation may go above the maximum allowed by the Classification Act of 1923, as amended.

9961.s: This order changes a Civil Service rule so the Civil Service Commission will decide how reemployment rights apply in general and in specific cases. It covers people who left federal service to serve in the armed forces of the United States or in the merchant marine. The Commission may also issue rules or instructions it thinks are needed to carry out those reemployment provisions.

9960.s: This order gives the Administrator for Economic Cooperation the duties the Secretary of State had for relief assistance to people of countries devastated by war. It also moves related personnel, records, property, and some available funds to the Economic Cooperation Administration, with budget approval needed for any fund transfer. The Administrator is also given the Secretary of State’s duties under the Foreign Aid Act of 1947 and must consult the Secretary before making or changing certain agreements.

9959.s: This order creates a Board of Inquiry to look into a labor dispute between the American Telephone and Telegraph Company’s Long Lines Division and some of its employees represented by the American Union of Telephone Workers. The order says the dispute could lead to a strike or lock-out affecting a substantial part of the communications industry. The Board must report to the President and then continue to carry out other duties under the law until the President ends it.

9957.s: This order takes control of the transportation systems of the railroad carriers named in the attached list and gives that control to the Secretary of the Army. The Secretary is directed to operate them to keep transportation service continuous and uninterrupted. It also lets the Secretary use public or private help, keep management in place when possible, and recognize workers’ rights to belong to labor organizations and bargain collectively under applicable law.

9958.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate a dispute between National Airlines, Inc. and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. From the date of the order and for thirty days after the report, National Airlines and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9955.s: This order changes promotion rules for commissioned officers in the Regular Corps of the Public Health Service. Officers in the nurse, dietitian, and therapist categories can be permanently promoted to the full and senior grades only if vacancies exist in those grades. Officers in the pharmacist and sanitarian categories can be permanently promoted to the senior grade only if a vacancy exists in that grade.

9952.s: This order ends certain reemployment rights to Federal service jobs for civilian employees who had transferred to public or private agencies for national-defense or war work. Those rights expire six months after the date of the order unless a reemployment application is made before then. The order does not affect reemployment rights gained under several later executive orders. The Civil Service Commission is allowed to set rules and procedures to carry out the order.

9953.s: This order creates an interdepartmental committee to help set up and promote a voluntary payroll savings plan for buying United States Savings Bonds, Series E. The plan is to be made available to officers and employees in executive branch departments, establishments, and agencies, and they are to be urged to participate. The committee also helps install the plan, shares information, and recommends improvements. This order replaces an earlier order from 1942 on the same kind of savings plan.

9951.s: This order restores a parcel of land in Honolulu, including its improvements, to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. The land had been reserved for the United States for military purposes, but the order says it was no longer needed for that use.

9950.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 9877 from July 26, 1947. That earlier order assigned primary functions and responsibilities to the three armed services.

9949.s: This order changes a prior executive order on transfers of personnel to certain public international organizations. It gives Paul D. Miles reemployment rights if he transfers from the Federal Communications Commission to the International Frequency Registration Board of the International Telecommunication Union and his service there ends without prejudice within five years. He must also meet the other requirements of the earlier order.

9948.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Aliquippa and Southern Railroad Company and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9947.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Pennsylvania Railroad and certain employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Enginemen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the railroad and its employees may not change the conditions involved except by agreement.

9946.s: This order sets rules for when certain travelers can be allowed transportation costs above the lowest first-class rate. It applies to people the Army, Air Force, Navy, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, Coast and Geodetic Survey, and Public Health Service may furnish transportation to, except certain military officers and civilian officers, employees, and their dependents. It allows higher-cost travel when the needed lower first-class accommodations were not available, when travelers paid for their own travel, and when a compartment or other approved accommodations are needed for security.

9945.s: This order changes a previous executive order about the Civil Service Retirement Act. It adds employees serving under emergency-indefinite appointments that do not exceed 5 years to the list of workers excluded from that retirement law.

9944.s: This order gives the Secretary of State the job of carrying out the President’s functions under two parts of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1948. It covers the International Children’s Emergency Fund Assistance Act of 1948 and the Greek-Turkish Assistance Act of 1948. It also says Title III must be administered under Executive Order No. 9857.

9942.s: This order gives the Secretary of Commerce and the Reconstruction Finance Corporation the power to carry out certain functions under the Rubber Act of 1948. It also lets them perform some of the President’s powers under that law, including subpoena power for the covered functions. The order took effect on April 1, 1948.

9943.s: This order authorizes the Administrator for Economic Cooperation to make allocations for the purposes of Titles I and IV of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1948, except section 404(b) of Title IV. It also says those functions may be carried out without following certain listed laws, and it applies to departments, agencies, and establishments of the Government involved in the act.

9941.s: This order lets the Secretary of State make rules for the Foreign Service Retirement and Disability System. It also lets the Secretary set rules for voluntary deposits into the Foreign Service Retirement and Disability Fund. It affects the Foreign Service retirement and disability system and the people who use it.

9938.s: This order revokes a 1945 order that had authorized the Secretary of War to take full control of a public airport on certain lands in Oregon. It affects the land described in the order, totaling 1,520 acres. The lease to the City of Redmond is meant to become active again and stay in force.

9937.s: This order lets several federal officials and agencies use authority that the President had under section 4 of the Philippine Property Act of 1946. It applies only to property in the Philippines that those agencies control and use for Title III of the Philippine Rehabilitation Act of 1946.

9939.s: This order creates a Board of Inquiry to look into a labor dispute between coal operators and certain employees represented by the International Union, United Mine Workers of America. The dispute involves wages or terms and conditions of employment in the bituminous coal industry, and the order says the strike affects a substantial part of that industry. The Board must report to the President and then stay in place to perform other duties under the law until the President ends it.

9936.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Terminal Railroad Association of St. Louis and certain of its employees. The dispute involves employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Enginemen, and the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days, and for that period, and for thirty days after the report, no changes may be made in the conditions that caused the dispute except by agreement.

9935.s: This order directs the Attorney General and the United States Maritime Commission to transfer certain vessels to the Government of Italy. It also directs the Maritime Commission to designate 15 surplus Liberty ships for transfer to Italy. The ships are to be operated by Italy for commercial use under the Italian flag, and they may not be sold to a non-Italian national without the consent of the United States.

9934-A.s: The order creates a Board of Inquiry to look into a labor dispute between several meat-packing companies and some of their employees represented by the United Packinghouse Workers of America. The dispute involves wages. The Board is to report to the President, and it may continue to serve under the Labor Management Relations Act until the President ends it.

9934.s: The order deals with a labor dispute between Carbide and Carbon Chemicals Corporation and some of its employees represented by the Atomic Trades and Labor Council, AFL, at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee. The dispute involves wages and terms and conditions of employment. It creates a Board of Inquiry to look into the dispute and report to the President. The Board may continue to perform other duties under the law until the President ends it.

9933.s: This order changes the rules for paying travel and moving expenses for civilian officers and employees of the United States when they are transferred to a new official station for permanent duty. It sets commuted rates for shipping household goods and personal effects within the continental United States and for temporary storage of those items. It also says government bills of lading shall not be used for these shipments.

9932.s: This order sets rules for certain government workers assigned to the Foreign Service. It says some people can be treated as having competitive status, and it gives certain Foreign Service staff officers and employees rights to be reinstated in their former agency. It also requires temporary hiring actions when a job is filled during a person's Foreign Service service, and it directs the Department of State to give advance notice before that service ends.

9930.s: This order authorizes and directs the publication of the 1949 edition of the Code of Federal Regulations in a special edition of the Federal Register. It covers the codification of documents that are in force and effect on December 31, 1948. Federal agencies under the Federal Register Act are asked to cooperate with the Division of the Federal Register in carrying out the order.

9931.s: This order changes a prior order about the National Security Resources Board. It names the Secretary of State, Treasury, Defense, Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, and Labor as members of the Board.

9928.s: This order suspends the requirement for professional examinations for permanent promotion in the Regular Army for officers in the Medical, Dental, and Veterinary Corps. The suspension lasts until June 30, 1948, and applies effective January 1, 1948.

9929.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a labor dispute between the Akron, Canton & Youngstown Railroad Company and other carriers and certain of their employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the carriers and employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9927.s: This order restores 8.82 acres of land near the Hilo Breakwater in Waiakea, South Hilo, Hawaii, to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. The land had been set aside for the United States Navy Department, but the order says it is no longer needed for Navy use. It affects the land that was formerly under Navy use and returns it to territorial control.

9926.s: This order amends a previous order that suspends the eight-hour law for laborers and mechanics employed by the Department of the Army or the Department of the Air Force on certain public works. It changes the condition for suspension so it applies when the Secretary of the Army or the Secretary of the Air Force finds it essential to the supply and maintenance of the military or naval forces.

9925.s: This order reserves the airspace over three United States Atomic Energy Commission facilities for national defense and other government purposes. It says no one may fly an aircraft in those areas unless it is for national defense or has authority from the Atomic Energy Commission. The three places are Clinton Engineering Works in Oak Ridge, Tennessee; Hanford Engineer Works in Richland, Washington; and the Los Alamos Project in Santa Fe, New Mexico. People who violate the order are subject to penalties under the Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938.

9923.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate a dispute between The Akron & Barberton Belt Railroad and certain employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the railroad and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9921.s: This order authorizes the Philippine Alien Property Administrator to transfer certain property, or the proceeds from it, to the Republic of the Philippines. The transfer can happen after claims, costs, and administration expenses are paid, or earlier if the Administrator decides it is administratively feasible and no substantial claims or expenses are likely. It applies to property vested in or transferred to the Administrator under the Trading with the Enemy Act and the Philippine Property Act of 1946.

9922.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate a dispute between the Chicago, North Shore & Milwaukee Railway Company and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days, and for that period and for thirty days after the report, neither side may change the conditions involved except by agreement.

9920.s: This order extends the trust periods and other restrictions on alienation for patents covering Indian lands that would otherwise expire during 1948. The extension is for 25 years from the date the trust would have expired. It does not apply to cases where Congress has reserved the authority to extend the trust period.

9919.s: This order delegates authority under the joint resolution to the Secretary of the Interior, the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of Commerce, and the Director of the Office of Defense Transportation. It lets them work on voluntary agreements, approvals, and written requests for compliance, but any agreement or plan must first be submitted to and approved by the Attorney General. It also gives these officials authority over fuels, agricultural commodities, scarce commodities, transportation facilities and equipment, and certain food and feed conservation powers.

9918.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate disputes between the Alabama, Tennessee and Northern Railroad Company and other listed carriers, and certain of their employees. It says the labor organizations may act as a unit in the board proceedings, and each carrier must be considered separately. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days, and no change may be made in the conditions out of which the disputes arose unless the parties agree.

9917.s: This order names several judges and attorneys as members, and one attorney as an alternate member, of military tribunals in the U.S. Zone of Occupation in Germany. These tribunals were set up to try and punish major war criminals of the European Axis. The order says the members may serve on any of the tribunals and that certain departments may provide them assistance and assign personnel to help with their duties.

9915.s: This order gives the Secretary of Agriculture the powers, authority, and discretion the President has under section 4(b) of the Joint Resolution approved December 30, 1947. It also changes earlier executive orders so they match this delegation.

9916.s: This order amends an earlier order about the National Capital Housing Authority. It says the authority will be made up of certain officials from the United States government or the District of Columbia government, plus two more officials named by the President. It affects the people who serve on that authority.

9914.s: This order gives the Secretary of State authority to carry out most of the powers under the Foreign Aid Act of 1947, with some actions needing agreement from other departments. It also says the field administrator must follow the Secretary of State’s guidance when running the aid program in recipient countries. The order transfers the funds for the act to the Department of State to be used under the act and the appropriation law.

9913.s: This order terminates the Office of Scientific Research and Development. It transfers the office’s personnel, property, contracts, records, funds, and functions to the National Military Establishment so its affairs can be fully liquidated. It also says the Director of the Bureau of the Budget may direct further steps needed to carry out the transfer.

9912.s:
This order creates the Interdepartmental Committee on Scientific Research and Development. The committee will include members from several federal departments and agencies, and the President will name its chairman each year.

The committee is directed to recommend ways to make federal research and development more effective, study administrative policies and practices, encourage cooperation among agencies, and suggest ways to share information about research. Federal agencies are asked to help the committee and provide information as allowed by law.

9911.s: This order designates the International Cotton Advisory Committee as a public international organization under the International Organizations Immunities Act. It gives the organization the privileges, exemptions, and immunities allowed by that law. The order says this does not reduce any other privileges or immunities the organization may have from treaty or congressional action.

9910.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Georgia Railroad and some of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Enginemen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the Georgia Railroad and its employees may not change the conditions tied to the dispute unless they agree to do so.

9908.s:
The order requires many sales, leases, permits, and other land deals involving land owned by the United States to reserve uranium, thorium, and other materials needed to make fissionable material for the United States. It also gives the United States the right to enter the land to prospect for, mine, and remove those materials, with just compensation for damage.

If the Atomic Energy Commission requires delivery of the material, it may take it and pay fair amounts for the work done before delivery. The reservation does not have to be included for land parcels of one acre or less that are mainly used as homes.

9909.s: This order exempts the District Court of the United States for Puerto Rico and the Department of Justice from making certain reports to the Coordinator of Federal agencies in Puerto Rico. It affects those two offices and removes the reporting requirement listed in the Organic Act of Puerto Rico.

9906.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 7165, which dealt with the preparation and publicity of decisions about overassessments of income, profits, estate, and gift taxes. It affects the handling of those decisions when they were allowed in excess of $20,000.

9907.s: This order closed many executive departments, agencies, and other government offices in the District of Columbia for one-half day on December 24, 1947. It also excused Federal employees in the District of Columbia and in the field service from duty for that half day, except for employees excluded for special public reasons or when their absence would conflict with existing law.

9905.s: The order names the Secretaries of the Treasury, Defense, Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, and Labor as members of the National Security Resources Board. It makes the chairman responsible for directing the board’s work and staff, including gathering facts and preparing reports on military, industrial, and civilian mobilization. It also requires federal departments and agencies to give the board information, reports, statistics, and other data, and to do studies and investigations the board asks for.

9903.s: This order ends the authority of the Secretary of Agriculture, the Reconstruction Finance Corporation and its Board of Directors, the United States Maritime Commission, and the Secretary of Commerce under earlier orders. It does not apply to articles entered for consumption, or taken from warehouse for consumption, before the 30th day after the order. It also changes any earlier executive orders that conflict with it.

9904.s: This order changes who would serve as Secretary of the Navy when the Secretary is temporarily absent. It sets the succession order as the Under Secretary of the Navy, the Assistant Secretary of the Navy for Air, the Assistant Secretary of the Navy, and the Chief of Naval Operations. It affects those Navy officers named in the succession list.

9902.s: This order approves an official seal for the Department of the Air Force. The seal includes a shield, a thunderbolt, an American bald eagle, an arc of thirteen stars, and the inscriptions "Department of the Air Force" and "United States of America."
