9900.s: The order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Railway Express Agency, Inc., and certain of its employees represented by Locals 459 and 808 of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, Chauffeurs, Warehousemen and Helpers of America, AFL. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. For thirty days after the board reports, the Railway Express Agency, Inc., and its employees may not change the conditions out of which the dispute arose except by agreement.

9899.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Atlanta & West Point Rail Road Company, the Western Railway of Alabama, and certain of their employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees cannot change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9898.s: This order suspends the eight-hour limit for laborers and mechanics employed by the Department of the Army or the Department of the Air Force on certain public works when the Secretary finds it essential. It applies to work needed for the supply and maintenance of the Army or the Air Force, essential construction, or international commitments. It says these workers are paid a basic day rate for eight hours, with overtime at time and one-half for hours over eight. It also supersedes a 1942 executive order.

9896.s: This order directs that the U.S. flag be flown at half-mast on two specific dates. It applies at all installations of the National Military Establishment, on public vessels in port, and on public buildings within the continental United States. The display is meant to honor memorial services for American soldiers, sailors, marines, and others who died in World War II.

9897.s: This order changes regulations for commissioned officers and employees of the Public Health Service. It updates rules for examinations, merit rolls, appointments, promotions, leave, and retirement. It also changes how service-connected disability is defined and when retired pay may continue for Reserve Corps officers.

9894.s: This order ends the San Clemente Island Naval Defensive Sea Area. That area had been established by earlier executive orders under authority in the Criminal Code.

9892.s: This order designates the Fish and Wildlife Service as the federal agency responsible for enforcing the Sockeye Salmon Fishery Act of 1947. It also covers enforcement of the 1930 U.S.-Canada convention on the sockeye salmon fishery and the regulations of the International Pacific Salmon Fisheries Commission. The service would do this under the direction of the Secretary of the Interior.

9891.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Railway Express Agency, Inc. and certain of its employees represented by the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, Chauffeurs, Warehousemen and Helpers of America, AFL. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. For thirty days after the report, and before that time, the company and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9890.s: This order changes the Quetico-Superior Committee’s authority over the wilderness sanctuary in the Rainy Lake and Pigeon River watersheds. It lets the committee consult and work with several federal departments, the State of Minnesota, and certain civic, scientific, educational, and conservation groups concerned with the area’s use and preservation. It also fills a vacancy on the committee by appointing Olaus J. Murie as a member.

9889.s: This order limits civil service exams for Substitute Railway Postal Clerk to people who are entitled to preference under the Veterans' Preference Act of 1944, as long as such people are available. It also lets some current employees in that position apply for classification and, if they qualify, receive competitive civil service status or probational status. Anyone who does not qualify under the order can be replaced from the competitive register.

9888.s: This order suspends compliance with certain laws about employment in the Canal Zone during any wars the United States is then engaged in or during the present national emergency. It also suspends, for fiscal year 1948, parts of those laws that require citizens of the Republic of Panama or the United States to be hired for skilled, technical, clerical, administrative executive, or supervisory jobs. The order says this action was needed because of a shortage of housing.

9887.s: This order designates the Preparatory Commission for the International Refugee Organization and its successor, the International Refugee Organization, as public international organizations under the International Organizations Immunities Act. It gives them the privileges, exemptions, and immunities allowed by that law. It also says those rights are not reduced if the organizations have other rights under treaty or congressional action.

9886.s: This order changes the rules for non-military and non-naval transportation on Army and Navy air transports. It replaces the time period of "two years and ten months" with "three years and one month" in one paragraph. It also says the order will stop later than that period if the Secretary of Defense sets different rules or orders.

9884.s: This order restores a small piece of land at Cocoanut Point in Hilo, Hawaii, to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. The land had been set aside for the United States for lighthouse purposes, but it is no longer needed for that use. It affects the land’s control between the United States and the Territory of Hawaii.

9885.s: This order says the Assistant Secretaries of Commerce may perform the duties of the Secretary of Commerce if the Secretary and the Under Secretary are absent, sick, resign, or die. It also says the Solicitor of Commerce may perform those duties if the Secretary, the Under Secretary, and the Assistant Secretaries are all unavailable. It replaces an earlier order on the same subject.

9883.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 9172, which had created a National Railway Labor Panel to help form emergency boards for railway labor disputes. It ends that panel and leaves handling of these disputes to the procedures under the Railway Labor Act.

9882.s: This order names three people to serve on one of the military tribunals set up in Germany to try and punish major war criminals of the European Axis. It says they may also serve on other military tribunals if the Military Governor of the United States Zone of Occupation directs it. The order also lets the Secretary of State, Secretary of War, Attorney General, and Secretary of the Navy provide assistance and assign personnel to help them carry out their duties.

9881.s: This order discontinues the Palmyra Island Naval Airspace Reservation and the Palmyra Island Naval Defensive Sea Area. It affects those two naval areas that were established in 1941.

9880.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the River Terminal Railway Company and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report is made, the company and its employees cannot change the conditions that led to the dispute except by agreement.

9877.s: This order assigns the main functions and responsibilities of the Army, Navy, and Air Force. It says the armed forces will defend the Constitution, protect the security of the United States, and conduct operations on land, at sea, and in the air. It also sets out each service’s role in training, equipment, joint operations, foreign service, and support for the other services.

9878.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Terminal Railroad Association of St. Louis and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report is made, neither side may change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9876.s: This order authorizes the Philippine Alien Property Administrator to carry out the President’s functions under section 101(b) of Reorganization Plan No. 1 of 1947. The administrator must do so subject to the President’s direction and control, and it applies to functions transferred to the President by that section.

9875.s: This order ends the military government in the former Japanese Mandated Islands and gives the Secretary of the Navy interim responsibility for civil administration of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. The Secretary of the Navy must carry out the United States' obligations under the agreement and the United Nations Charter, working with other federal departments or agencies when needed. Decisions about closing areas for security reasons must be made jointly by the Secretary of the Navy and the Secretary of State. The order stays in effect until a civilian department or agency is chosen to have permanent responsibility for the government of the trust territory.

9873.s: This order transfers the War Department’s functions for administering the Mexico City National Cemetery to the American Battle Monuments Commission. It also transfers related civilian personnel, records, supplies, equipment, property, and certain unexpended funds. The change affects the administration of that cemetery and the people and resources tied to it.

9874.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate disputes between three railroad companies and some of their employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the carriers and employees may not change the working conditions involved unless they agree to do so.

9872.s: This order changes a previous order about land at the Fort De Russy Military Reservation in Hawaii. It removes the United States' right to build a railroad on the land that was restored to the Territory of Hawaii. It affects that parcel of land and the government's reserved railroad right.

9871.s: This order sets rules for quarters and subsistence allowances for enlisted men in the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard who are not given quarters or rations in kind. It also covers per diem allowances for members of those services, plus the Coast and Geodetic Survey and Public Health Service, when they are on duty outside the continental United States or in Alaska. It gives certain enlisted men with dependents money allowances for quarters when public quarters are not available, and it replaces several earlier executive orders.

9870.s: This order lets the Secretary of State set rules for granting and paying certain allowances under the Foreign Service Act of 1946. It also lets the Secretary of State set rules for accounting for those allowances and for allotments of funds under that Act. The order confirms earlier State Department regulations on these matters and applies to Foreign Service officers and employees who are U.S. citizens.

9869.s: This order changes the clothing allowance rules for enlisted personnel in the Navy, the Coast Guard, the Naval Reserve, and the Coast Guard Reserve. It updates the amounts paid for clothing in kind or as cash allowances and makes the changes effective July 1, 1947, through the fiscal year ending June 30, 1948.

9867.s: This order changes a part of the rules for non-military and non-naval transportation on Army and Navy air transports. It replaces the words "two years and eight months" with "two years and ten months" in paragraph 2(c) of the earlier order.

9868.s: This order designates two people to serve on military tribunals in the United States Zone of Occupation in Germany. The tribunals were set up to try and punish major war criminals of the European Axis. The Secretary of State, Secretary of War, Attorney General, and Secretary of the Navy may provide assistance and assign personnel to help them do their duties.

9865.s: This order directs federal departments and agencies to try to get the right to file foreign patent applications for inventions from government research. It also directs the Department of Commerce to decide where to seek patent protection, manage foreign patents, and issue licenses under the rules in the order. The Department of State is to negotiate arrangements with other governments for access to foreign patents. Inventions under the Atomic Energy Commission and inventions classified as secret or confidential for national security are exempt.

9866.s: This order sets who will perform the duties of the Secretary of the Interior if the Secretary is dead, resigns, is absent, or is sick. It names the Under Secretary first, then the ranking Assistant Secretary or other Assistant Secretary present, and then the Solicitor of the Department of the Interior if the others cannot serve. It also says which Assistant Secretary counts as the ranking Assistant Secretary and replaces a prior order.

9863.s: This order designates three international organizations as public international organizations under the International Organizations Immunities Act. The organizations named are the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, the International Civil Aviation Organization, and the International Telecommunication Union. It says these organizations are entitled to the privileges, exemptions, and immunities given by that law, and that this does not limit any other privileges or immunities they may have by treaty or congressional action.

9864.s: This order sets rules for carrying out a joint resolution that provides relief assistance to people in countries devastated by war. It gives the Secretary of State authority to use most of the powers in the resolution, except for appointing the field administrator. The field administrator must follow the guidance and instructions of the Secretary of State.

9862.s: This order allows certain civilian employees in the Executive branch of the Federal Government to be transferred to the American Mission for Aid to Greece or the American Mission for Aid to Turkey. The transfer must be requested by the Secretary of State or an authorized representative, and it must have the employee’s consent and the consent of the department or agency head. It also applies existing rules for transferring personnel to public international organizations to these transfers.

9860.s: This order restores one parcel of land at Sand Island, Oahu, Hawaii, to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. That land is to be used in connection with the construction of the Keehi Lagoon Seaplane Harbor. It also makes another parcel subject to an easement for the Territory of Hawaii to build and maintain a breakwater, while the War Department keeps its use of that parcel.

9859.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 9196, which was titled "Government Purchases of Prison-made Goods." It ends that earlier order’s rules about government purchases of prison-made goods.

9861.s: This order returns two parcels of land from the Fort Armstrong Military Reservation in Oahu, Hawaii, to the use of the Territory of Hawaii for road purposes. The territory may remove or destroy buildings or other improvements on those lands, but it must pay the costs, repair any damage to nearby U.S. property, and pay for any removed or destroyed improvements that cannot be repaired. It also modifies two earlier executive orders.

9858.s: This order designates four people to serve on a military tribunal in the United States Zone of Occupation within Germany. The tribunal is for the trial and punishment of major war criminals of the European Axis. It also allows the named officials to receive compensation and allows certain Cabinet members to provide them assistance and assign personnel to help with their duties.

9857-B.s: This order changes the rules for the President's Certificate of Merit. It says the award cannot be given for acts or service done after the end of hostilities of World War II, and proposals submitted after June 30, 1947, will not be considered by the Medal for Merit Board.

9857-A.s: This order changes the rules for awarding the Medal for Merit. It says the medal may be awarded only by the President or at his direction to certain civilians of nations prosecuting the war and other friendly foreign nations for exceptionally meritorious conduct or courageous acts in support of the war effort. It also creates a three-member Medal for Merit Board to review proposals and make recommendations to the President, and it bars awards for services after the stated end of hostilities and proposals submitted after June 30, 1947.

9855.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Bingham & Garfield Railway Company and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9857.s: This order sets rules for carrying out the act that provides assistance to Greece and Turkey. It authorizes the Secretary of State to use powers given to the President under the act, including spending funds made available for it. The Chief of Mission to Greece or Turkey is to direct U.S. activities there under the Secretary of State's guidance, and other government departments are to help provide personnel, supplies, facilities, and services when needed.

9853.s: This order lets commissioned officers of the Coast and Geodetic Survey who are on duty outside the continental United States or in Alaska be paid actual and necessary expenses, or per diem instead. The payment may be equal to what the Secretary of the Navy authorizes for commissioned officers of the Navy.

9852.s: This order designates Charles F. Wennerstrum as a member of one of the military tribunals in the United States Zone of Occupation in Germany. Those tribunals were set up for the trial and punishment of major war criminals of the European Axis. It also lets the Secretary of State, Secretary of War, Attorney General, and Secretary of the Navy provide help and assign personnel to assist him in his duties.

9854.s: This order transfers a tract of land, with its improvements, from the Department of the Interior to the Veterans' Administration. The land is part of the Phoenix Indian School Reserve at Phoenix, Arizona, and the transfer affects that property and its control.

9851.s: This order adds a tract of federally owned land, about 263.70745 acres, to the Mount Vernon Memorial Highway. The land was under the control of the Administrator of Civil Aeronautics, but the order says that office no longer needs it. The added land will be administered by the National Park Service in the Department of the Interior.

9849.s: This order suspends the eight-hour work limit for laborers and mechanics employed by the Alaska Railroad on public work in Alaska, for six months. It applies when the Secretary of the Interior finds the suspension is needed to carry out the order. It also says their pay must be based on a 40-hour workweek, with overtime paid at time and one-half for hours over 40 in a week.

9850.s: This order changes the rules for glider flights by qualified personnel of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard, including those in training. It requires them to perform one or more glider flights during any three consecutive calendar months if ordered to participate regularly and frequently. It also allows different compliance periods when glider equipment, towing aircraft, or combat conditions make the required flights impossible, and it gives a temporary exception for someone who becomes unable to fly because of an aviation accident.

9847.s: This order ends the Solid Fuels Administrator’s authority immediately and abolishes the Solid Fuels Administration for War at the close of business on June 30, 1947. It also revokes the earlier order that created the agency. The Secretary of the Interior is authorized to wind up and liquidate the agency’s affairs using its personnel, property, records, and funds, and any other funds that are appropriated for that purpose.

9848.s: This order directs the United States Maritime Commission to dispose of certain foreign merchant vessels that are no longer needed by the United States. Before any vessel is disposed of, the Secretary of State must find that it is consistent with the foreign policies of the United States, and the Attorney General must find that it will not harm the interests of the United States in any related litigation. Money from the sale or return of the vessels, after expenses, must be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts.

9845.s: This order changes an earlier rule that limited federal officers and employees from holding state or local offices. It allows employees of the Bureau of Reclamation, with approval from the Secretary of the Interior, to accept appointments as constables or deputy sheriffs in the states or territories where they are working. Their service in those roles must be unpaid and must not interfere with their Bureau of Reclamation duties.

9843.s: The order authorizes the Secretary of the Navy to transfer certain naval vessels, craft, and floating drydocks to the Republic of China without compensation. It also allows the Navy to repair and equip them, transfer needed nonsecret material, train personnel, and detail up to one hundred officers and two hundred enlisted men to assist in naval matters. These actions must follow the 1946 law and need the Secretary of State’s concurrence.

9841.s: This order ends the Office of Temporary Controls and sets out how its work and records will be handled. It moves rent control functions to the Housing Expediter, rice price control to the Secretary of Agriculture, and several other functions to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation and the Secretary of Commerce. It also revokes one earlier executive order and withdraws authority for compulsory orders for products or materials.

9842.s: This order authorizes the Attorney General to coordinate and handle certain lawsuits for the United States. It covers cases for the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of Commerce, and the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, as well as cases against violators of price rules for commodities removed from price control. It also covers litigation tied to subsidy withholding under Directive 41.

9840.s: This order changes an earlier rule on non-military and non-naval transportation on Army and Navy air transports. It replaces the words "two and one-half years" with "two years and eight months."

9839.s: This order transfers back to the Federal Works Administrator the functions, powers, and duties tied to the Grand River Dam Project that had been given to the Secretary of the Interior. It also transfers the related bonds, contracts, records, and accounts used in running those duties. The Secretary of the Interior keeps authority to finish the settlement of accounts with the Grand River Dam Authority and the work on acquiring an additional five feet of reservoir storage for the project.

9836.s: This order moves the functions, duties, and powers for the Veterans' Emergency Housing Program from the Civilian Production Administration to the Housing Expediter. It also allows the Housing Expediter to use certain presidential powers for that program and to use designated personnel, property, records, and funds from the Office of Temporary Controls. Prior conflicting executive orders and other related agency rules are changed as needed.

9835.s: This order sets up loyalty investigations for people entering civilian jobs in the executive branch and for employees already working there. It requires departments and agencies to use hearings, notices, and appeals before removing someone for disloyalty, and it creates a Loyalty Review Board in the Civil Service Commission to review cases and coordinate loyalty policies. It also tells agencies to gather and share loyalty-related information, keep a central index of investigated persons, and sets standards for conduct that may count as disloyalty.

9838.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate disputes between four railroad companies and certain of their employees represented by the national Maritime Union, C.I.O. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the companies and their employees may not change the conditions that led to the disputes except by agreement.

9833.s: This order makes certain corporation tax returns open to inspection by the Federal Trade Commission. It covers income, excess-profits, declared value excess-profits, and capital stock tax returns for the listed tax years, along with related statistical transcript cards. The inspection must follow rules set by the Secretary of the Treasury.

9834.s: This order applies travel and transportation expense rules to civilian officers and employees, and to their immediate families, household goods, and personal effects, when departmental functions are returned to the seat of government. It applies only to officers and employees whose positions were transferred to the seat of government after October 11, 1944. It also revokes Executive Order No. 9739, with an exception for certain incomplete returns ordered before November 1, 1946.

9831.s: This order abolishes the Board of War Communications and transfers its property and records to the Federal Communications Commission. It also revokes five earlier executive orders that had created or changed that board. The change affects the federal agencies named in the order.

9830.s: This order amends the Civil Service Rules and sets out how federal personnel administration will work. It gives the Civil Service Commission responsibility for applying civil service laws and rules, setting standards, and reviewing agency personnel actions. It also makes agency heads responsible for personnel management in their own agencies and sets rules for competitive examinations, appointments, and competitive status in the federal service.

9832.s: The order sets procedures for how trade agreements are handled under the Trade Agreements Act of 1934. It requires trade agreements to include a clause that lets the United States withdraw or modify a concession if increased imports threaten serious injury to domestic producers. It also creates an Interdepartmental Committee on Trade Agreements to gather information and advise the President, and it requires analyses of import and export items before trade agreement recommendations are made.

9829.s: This order extends the provisions of Executive Order 9177 to the United States Atomic Energy Commission. It also lets the Commission perform the functions and powers given in that order to the Secretary of War, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Agriculture, and the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, for articles entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption on or after January 1, 1947.

9828.s: This order transfers the Surplus Property Office of the Department of the Interior to the War Assets Administration. It also transfers related records, funds, property, contracts, obligations, and personnel used mainly for those duties. The two agencies may continue to supply each other materials, equipment, work, and services, and the War Assets Administrator may end the office as a separate unit.

9827.s: The order appoints three members and one alternate member to a military tribunal in the United States Zone of Occupation within Germany. The tribunal is for the trial and punishment of major war criminals of the European Axis. The named members may also serve on other military tribunals in that zone if the Military Governor directs, and several federal departments are authorized to help them with their duties.

9825.s: This order amends rules for allowances for quarters and subsistence for enlisted men traveling on duty. It sets daily payments when sleeping car, stateroom, quarters, or rations are not provided, and it gives lower allowances when some quarters or meals are furnished. It also says men with temporary detentions during travel are treated as traveling under orders for the whole period, and that after the thirty-first day of detention, Section I applies.

9824.s: This order amends a prior executive order to add a new group of workers to the exclusions from the Civil Service Retirement Act. It applies to consular agents appointed under section 551 of the Foreign Service Act of 1946.

9823.s: This order designates the Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees and the International Wheat Advisory Committee, also called the International Wheat Council, as public international organizations under the International Organizations Immunities Act. It says these organizations are entitled to the privileges, exemptions, and immunities given by that law. The order also says it does not reduce any other privileges or immunities they may have under treaty or congressional action.

9821.s: This order changes a prior order about the National Housing Agency. It removes the language saying the National Housing Administrator would receive a salary of $12,000 a year unless Congress decides otherwise, and leaves the appointment to the President with the Senate’s advice and consent. It is effective as of December 15, 1946.

9822.s: This order directs the U.S. Maritime Commission to return certain Finnish merchant vessels to their former owners or their successors. The return must be made under an agreement that lets the Commission offset the fair and reasonable value of the vessels against the compensation owed for taking them. Questions about the final compensation are left to later determination under the agreement and applicable law.

9819.s: This order designates three people as members and one person as an alternate member of a military tribunal in the United States Zone of Occupation within Germany. The tribunal was set up to try and punish major war criminals of the European Axis. The order also says the designated people may receive support, personnel, and compensation while carrying out their duties.

9820.s: This order separates the Housing Expediter’s powers, duties, and functions from the National Housing Administrator. It makes the Housing Expediter an independent officer of the government. It also transfers related personnel, assets, contracts, records, and some funds to the Office of the Housing Expediter.

9818.s: This order sets up the Philippine Alien Property Administration in the Executive Office of the President and puts it under a Philippine Alien Property Administrator appointed by the President. It gives that administrator rights, powers, duties, and functions over property located in the Philippines and property transferred under the order. It also lets the Attorney General transfer property, personnel, records, and supplies to the new administration, and requires the administrator to consult with the Secretary of State before vesting any property or interest.

9817.s: This order sets rules for cash awards to civilian federal employees and former employees for suggestions that are adopted and lead to savings, better service, or other improvements. It also allows departments to give certificates, medals, or other emblems for exceptional or meritorious service. It says awards are not paid for suggestions that are part of normal job duties or are not used within five years.

9815.s: This order changes a rule about who may keep working under the authority of Section 7 of Executive Order 9691 after the general revision of Schedule A is issued. It says a person may not continue in that employment unless the position is included under Schedule A, and it does not apply to positions held by people with classified competitive civil service status.

9816.s: This order transfers United States property connected to atomic energy and fissionable material to the Atomic Energy Commission. It also transfers property and records of the Manhattan Engineer District, with some records able to be excepted if the Secretary of War and the Commission agree or if the President decides. It moves civilian officers and employees of the Manhattan Engineer District to the Commission, while military and naval personnel continue to be made available for duty there by agreement.

9814.s: This order creates a three-member President’s Amnesty Board. The board must review cases of people convicted under the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, including violations of rules under that law and conspiracies to violate it. It may send findings and recommendations to the Attorney General about whether executive clemency should be granted or denied. Federal departments and agencies must cooperate with the board and give it information and help.

9812.s: This order makes income, excess-profits, and declared value excess-profits tax returns for 1941, 1942, and 1943 open to inspection by the House Committee on Naval Affairs, or a duly authorized subcommittee. The inspection must follow rules and regulations set by the Secretary of the Treasury. It is to be used to carry out House Resolution 154.

9813.s: This order names three members and one alternate member for a military tribunal in the United States Zone of Occupation within Germany. The tribunal is for the trial and punishment of major war criminals of the European Axis. It also authorizes the Secretary of State, the Secretary of War, the Attorney General, and the Secretary of the Navy to provide assistance and assign personnel to help them do their duties.

9810.s: This order closed federal offices in the District of Columbia for one-half day on December 24, 1946, the day before Christmas Day. It also excused most Federal employees in the District of Columbia and in the field service from duty for that half day. Some employees could be excluded by their department heads or because their absence would conflict with existing law.

9811.s: This order extends the trust periods, or other limits on sale, for patents applying to Indian lands that would expire during calendar year 1947. The extension is for 25 more years from the date the trust would otherwise end. It applies to both tribal and individual Indian lands, except where Congress has kept the authority to extend the trust period for itself.

9809.s: This order combines several wartime agencies into one new office called the Office of Temporary Controls. It also moves many functions from agencies like the Office of War Mobilization and Reconversion, the Office of Price Administration, and the National Wage Stabilization Board to other parts of the government. The order affects those agencies, their boards, and the personnel, records, property, and funds tied to the functions being moved.

9808.s: This order creates the President's Committee on Civil Rights. The committee is told to look into whether current law enforcement measures and the powers of federal, state, and local governments can be strengthened to safeguard the civil rights of the people. Federal departments and agencies must cooperate, and their employees may be asked to testify and provide documents. The committee must report to the President and then end unless the President later keeps it going.

9807.s: This order authorizes the Civil Service Commission to give competitive civil service status to certain current or former federal employees. It applies to people who were in listed groups of positions on July 1, 1941, and who stayed in government service through January 1, 1942. The covered groups include positions paid from funds for the Civilian Conservation Corps, the Public Works Administration, certain emergency relief work, and the Northeast Timber Salvage Administration.

9806.s: This order creates the President's Temporary Commission on Employee Loyalty. The commission will study rules for investigating people who work for the United States Government or apply for those jobs, and for removing or disqualifying disloyal or subversive people. It also directs executive departments and agencies to cooperate and give the commission information and witnesses. The commission must report its findings and recommendations to the President by February 1, 1947, and then it ends unless extended by another executive order.

9804.s: This order revokes two older executive orders about how employees' compensation is handled for Alaska Railroad employees. It moves administration of the Employees' Compensation Act for those employees to the Federal Security Agency. The order takes effect on January 1, 1947.

9805.s: This order sets rules for paying travel and transportation expenses when civilian federal employees are transferred from one official station to another for permanent duty. It covers the employee, the employee’s immediate family, and shipment of household goods and personal effects, with limits on weight and storage time. It also says some items cannot be included, such as wines, liquors, animals or birds not needed for official duties, and automobiles. The order revokes several earlier executive orders and makes these rules effective as of November 1, 1946.

9803.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Lehigh Valley Railroad Company and certain of its employees. The dispute involves the Brotherhood of Railway and Steamship Clerks, Freight Handlers, Express and Station Employees, and the board must report to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees may not change the conditions that led to the dispute except by agreement.

9802.s: This order changes the rules for payment certificates under section 124(h) of the Internal Revenue Code. It says a payment certificate will be issued only if the application is filed under the regulations on or before December 31, 1946. It affects people applying for these payment certificates.

9799.s: This order gives the Secretary of State the President’s authority to classify the positions that are to be occupied by chiefs of mission into four classes. It applies to the internal management of the government and takes effect on November 13, 1946.

9801.s: This order ends the wage and salary controls that were in effect under the Stabilization Act of 1942. It also says those old rules still apply for offenses, rights, or liabilities that happened before the order date. It affects wages and salaries under those earlier executive orders and regulations.

9798.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Barre & Chelsea Railroad Company, the St. Johnsbury & Lake Champlain Railroad Company, and certain of their employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. For that time, and for thirty days after the report is made, the companies and their employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9797.s: This order transfers certain air-navigation facilities, property, equipment, supplies, and related functions in Alaska and other places outside the continental United States from the War and Navy Departments to the Department of Commerce. It applies only to facilities no longer needed for military purposes that Commerce finds necessary for safe and efficient civil aircraft use. Commerce is directed to operate and maintain the transferred property, and the War or Navy Department may take back any transferred facilities if military necessity requires it.

9796.s: This order changes a prior executive order about captured enemy flags, standards, and colors. It adds a rule that such items taken by the Marine Corps, if not already under the care of the Superintendent of the United States Naval Academy and unless the Secretary of the Navy directs otherwise, must be deposited for preservation and display at the United States Marine Corps Museum in Quantico, Virginia. The museum’s Curator would have care of them.

9795.s: This order restores certain land at Mala Landing, Lahaina, Maui, Hawaii, to the jurisdiction of the Territory of Hawaii. The land had been set aside for use by the United States Navy Department as a section base and radio station, but it is no longer needed for that use. It applies to the described parcel of land on Maui.

9794.s: This order lets the Solicitor of the Department of the Interior act as the Under Secretary of the Interior. It also lets the Solicitor or an Assistant Secretary act in place of the Under Secretary or an Assistant Secretary if that person dies, resigns, is absent, or is sick.

9792.s: This order changes Executive Order 9492, which sets rules for non-military and non-naval transportation on Army and Navy air transports. It replaces words in section 2(c) with new wording about a time period of "tow and one-half years."

9791.s: This order directs a study of scientific research and development done or paid for by federal agencies and by non-federal groups. It asks for information on the fields of research, the personnel and facilities needed, and the costs involved. It also creates the President's Scientific Research Board to help with the study and to advise on reports to the President.

9793.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate disputes between the Atlanta & St. Andrews Bay Railway Company, other listed carriers, and certain employees represented by listed railway labor organizations. Each carrier is to be considered separately, and the labor organizations may act as a unit in the board proceedings. The board must report its findings to the President, and no change may be made in the disputed working conditions except by agreement during the period set in the order.

9790.s: This order changes the boundaries of the Wheeler National Wildlife Refuge. It removes one tract of land in Morgan County, Alabama from the refuge and ends the Department of the Interior’s right to use that land, with jurisdiction returning to the Tennessee Valley Authority. It also lets the Department and the Authority agree to remove other lands from the refuge in the future if they certify the change is in the public interest and consistent with the listed laws.

9788.s: This order ends the Office of Alien Property Custodian and moves its powers and duties to the Attorney General. It also transfers the office’s property, records, personnel, and funds to the Department of Justice. The Attorney General will handle the property and other functions through officers and agencies he designates.

9789.s: This order ends the Office of Alien Property Custodian and gives its authority and functions to the Attorney General. It also transfers the office’s property, personnel, records, and funds to the Department of Justice. The Attorney General is to manage these duties through officers and agencies of the Department of Justice he designates.

9787.s: This order establishes the waters around San Clemente Island, California, as a naval defensive sea area for national defense. It sets the covered water area and says vessels or other craft may not enter unless authorized by the Secretary of the Navy. Anyone who breaks the order is subject to legal penalties.

9786.s: This order sets rules for filing and handling claims by contractors and subcontractors against government departments and agencies under Public Law 657. It explains who may file, what information must be included, and when claims must be submitted. It also directs war agencies, the General Accounting Office, and other agencies on how to review, settle, and report on these claims.

9785.s: This order amends a previous rule on clothing for enlisted Navy and Coast Guard personnel, including reserve members. It adds a new section for enlisted members of the Women's Reserve of the Naval Reserve and the Women's Reserve of the Coast Guard Reserve. After reenlisting and reporting for active duty more than three months after discharge, they are entitled to a $200 cash allowance instead of clothing and a $12.50 quarterly clothing maintenance allowance under the stated terms.

9784.s: This order requires federal agencies to keep only records needed for current work and to offer other records for transfer to the National Archives or other lawful disposition. It also limits transfers between agencies unless approved by the Director of the Bureau of the Budget, with special rules for personnel records and confidential records. The order applies to executive departments, independent establishments, and certain government corporations, and it covers many kinds of government records.

9783.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 7744, which had let the Solicitor of the Department of Labor act as Secretary of Labor in some cases when the Secretary was absent. It says that the new law in the Department of Labor provides that the Under Secretary of Labor will perform those duties when the Secretary is absent.

9782.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Utah Idaho Central Railroad Corporation and certain of its employees represented by the International Association of Machinists. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report is made, the railroad and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute unless they agree to do so.

9781.s: This order creates the Air Coordinating Committee to help coordinate aviation policies and activities among federal agencies. It includes representatives from the State, War, Post Office, Navy, and Commerce Departments, plus the Civil Aeronautics Board. The committee is directed to study aviation problems, recommend policies, consult with other federal aviation groups, and report unresolved issues and yearly activities to the President.

9776.s: This order reopens East Executive Avenue in the District of Columbia to public travel. It says the road is to be open on and after September 9, 1946.

9775.s: This order establishes the Federal Committee on Highway Safety. The committee is made up of representatives from several Federal agencies and a chairman designated by the President, or by the Federal Works Administrator if that authority is delegated. It is directed to promote highway safety, reduce highway traffic accidents, encourage cooperation with State and local governments and highway safety organizations, and coordinate Federal highway safety activities where allowed by law.

9774.s: This order designates the Reconstruction Finance Corporation to sell, exchange, or otherwise dispose of certain bonds, notes, and other securities tied to loans made to the Georgia and Florida Railway Company. It also lets the corporation arrange to extend the maturity of those securities on terms it thinks are advisable and in the public interest. Any money made from this authority must be paid to the Secretary of the Treasury. The order also amends a prior executive order.

9772.s: This order ends the suspension of punishment limits for certain military offenses committed in occupied enemy territory after the order took effect. It applies to violations of Articles of War 58, 59, 61, and 86, including desertion, aiding desertion, absence without leave, and misbehavior of sentinels. Punishments for those offenses in occupied enemy territory are again subject to the maximum limits in the Army courts-martial manual.

9771.s: This order transfers the use, possession, and control of a 7.33-acre tract of land in Washington County, Tennessee, to the Tennessee Valley Authority. It also transfers any United States interest in the north half of U.S. Highway 11E next to that tract. The Veterans' Administration no longer needs the land.

9768.s: This order extends the provisions of Executive Order 9177 to the Secretary of Commerce. It lets the Secretary of Commerce carry out the functions and powers given by that order to the Secretary of War, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Agriculture, and the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, for articles entered or withdrawn for consumption on or after August 1, 1946.

9769.s: This order changes the rules for appointing fourth-class postmasters. It raises the pay limit from $500 to $1,000 for appointments that may be made without the competitive Civil Service Rules. It affects appointments to these postmaster jobs where the compensation is within that limit.

9767.s: This order amends the fee schedule for United States Foreign Service services. It changes the fee for a certified copy of an executed repatriation form for native-born American women and removes one fee exception. It also says there is no fee for administering the oath of allegiance in two listed cases, including certain people who lost citizenship through military service and native-born women who lost citizenship by marriage to an alien.

9766.s: The order lets the Secretary of War temporarily assign an Army officer to military duty with the Institute of Inter-American Affairs and the Inter-American Educational Foundation. The officer keeps all Army rights, benefits, promotions, and status while detailed.

9764.s: This order opens certain tax returns from 1939 to 1945 to inspection by a special Senate committee and any authorized subcommittee. The returns include income, excess-profits, declared value excess-profits, and capital stock tax returns. The committee may use them for its work on the national-defense program, subject to the stated Treasury conditions.

9762.s: This order transfers the Office of Economic Stabilization, along with its functions, records, property, personnel, and funds, to the Office of War Mobilization and Reconversion. It also transfers the powers of the Economic Stabilization Director to the Director of War Mobilization and Reconversion. The Economic Stabilization Board is moved for the purpose of advising and consulting with that director, and earlier rules stay in effect unless they conflict with this order or are changed later.

9761.s: This order directs the Secretary of the Navy to have flags, standards, and colors taken by the Navy from enemies of the United States in war deposited for preservation and display at the United States Naval Academy. It also says the same kind of items taken by the Coast Guard while operating as part of the Navy must be deposited at the United States Coast Guard Academy. The order supersedes a 1849 order on the same subject.

9763.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate a dispute between the Pullman Company and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the board reports, Pullman Company and its employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9759.s: This order suspends compliance with certain employment rules in the Canal Zone that are found in three 1947 appropriation acts. The suspension lasts during any wars the United States is then engaged in and during the present national emergency.

9760.s: This order gives the Secretary of State authority over diplomatic and consular property in the United States that is owned or controlled by Germany or Japan, including the assets on those premises. It says the Alien Property Custodian and the Secretary of the Treasury must stop controlling that property when the Secretary of State takes action and gives written notice. The Secretary of State may also issue rules and instructions to carry out the order.

9752.s: This order restores a piece of land on Sand Island in Hawaii to the Territory of Hawaii for the use of the City and County of Honolulu. The land is to be used to build a sewage-treatment plant. The War Department may approve plans that affect present or future Army installations, and it gets free sewage disposal and treatment up to a total of $100,000 if charges are later imposed on users.

9758.s: This order authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to take possession of and operate the Carter Coal Company mines in McDowell County, West Virginia, along with related property and assets needed to run them. It directs the Secretary to keep the mines operating, handle coal production and distribution, and work within the terms and conditions of employment in place when possession is taken. It also says employees may keep their labor organization membership, bargain collectively, and take part in concerted activities if they do not interfere with mine operations, and it directs federal agencies to help as much as possible.

9751.s: This order designates several international organizations as public international organizations that can receive the privileges, exemptions, and immunities given by the International Organizations Immunities Act. It applies to the Inter-American Coffee Board, the Inter-American Institute of Agricultural Sciences, the Inter-American Statistical Institute, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the International Monetary Fund, and the Pan American Sanitary Bureau. It also says this does not reduce any privileges and immunities those organizations already have or may get by treaty or congressional action.

9750.s: This order removes certain training positions in government hospitals from the Classification Act of 1923. It covers medical and dental interns and residents-in-training, student nurses, student dietitians, student physical therapists, student occupational therapists, and other people assigned mainly for training in those hospitals, clinics, or laboratories. Their pay and other allowances will be set by the responsible department heads or the District of Columbia commissioners, with Civil Service Commission approval of the maximum rates.

9749.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate a dispute between the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad Company and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days, and for that period and for thirty days after the report, no change may be made in the disputed conditions except by agreement.

9748.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate a dispute between Northwest Airlines and certain of its employees represented by the International Association of Machinists. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. Northwest Airlines and its employees may not change the conditions in dispute except by agreement during that time and for thirty days after the board reports.

9747.s: This order keeps certain existing executive orders in force in the Philippines after July 4, 1946. It lets the Alien Property Custodian and the Secretary of the Treasury keep exercising the powers given to them there under those orders.

9745.s: This order directs the Office of Price Administration and the Price Administrator to keep carrying out certain functions, powers, and duties that did not end with the termination of the Emergency Price Control Act and the Stabilization Act. It also keeps existing orders, regulations, and directives in force until they are changed or revoked by proper authority. The order does not authorize the office to set or keep rules on current prices or rents unless later legislation provides for it.

9746.s: This order lets the Secretary of War and the Governor of the Panama Canal carry out many powers over the Panama Canal and the Canal Zone. It covers rules on canal operations, ships, aircraft, health and quarantine, taxes, alcohol, hiring and pay, travel into the Canal Zone, and military and naval reservations. It also gives the Governor authority over roads and highways, some local law enforcement matters, boxing or sparring rules, and the public defender.

9744-C.s: This order changes an earlier rule about allowances for quarters and subsistence for enlisted men who are not furnished quarters or rations in kind. It keeps that earlier order in effect until June 30, 1947, unless it is changed or revoked sooner.

9744-B.s: This order sets rules for clothing in kind and cash clothing allowances for enlisted personnel of the Navy, Coast Guard, Naval Reserve, and Coast Guard Reserve. It says when these allowances are payable, when they are not payable, and how they work for reenlistment, recall, transfers, and certain rank changes. It also sets quarterly maintenance allowances and gives members of the Women's Reserve of the Coast Guard Reserve a special quarterly clothing allowance of $12.50.

9744-A.s: This order transfers the Review Committee on Deferment of Government Employees to the Office of War Mobilization and Reconversion and to the Director of War Mobilization and Reconversion. It also transfers the committee’s functions, records, property, personnel, funds, and the Secretary of Labor’s related functions. It says existing rules and directives tied to those functions stay in effect unless they conflict with this order or are later changed or revoked.

9744.s: This order ends the Office of the Director of Liquidation and the Liquidation Advisory Committee, along with their functions. It also directs the Director of the Bureau of the Budget to handle the records and property in the possession of the Director of Liquidation, in line with applicable law.

9743.s: This order applies the same regulations for paying transportation expenses of immediate family members to civilian officers and employees covered by the 1947 appropriation act. It covers transfers from one official station to another for permanent duty, when the move is authorized by the head of the department or establishment.

9742.s: This order ends the War Relocation Authority as an organization within the Department of the Interior and abolishes the office of its director. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to wind up the Authority’s affairs and use its personnel, records, property, and funds as needed. It also changes any prior executive orders that conflict with this order.

9740.s: This order changes the leave rules for full-time employees of the Panama Canal and the Panama Railroad Company on the Isthmus of Panama. It sets rules for annual leave, travel leave, sick leave, leave without pay, lump-sum payments when an employee separates or dies, and the Governor's authority to make related regulations. It also gives special leave rules for policemen, firemen, teachers, and certain alien employees, and revokes a prior order that had authorized sick and rest leave for alien employees.

9741.s: This order extends the life of the Quantico-Superior Committee for four more years. The extension runs from June 30, 1946, to June 30, 1950. It affects the committee created by Executive Order No. 6783.

9738.s: This order restricts civil-service examinations for Correctional Officer jobs in the Bureau of Prisons to people entitled to preference under the Veterans' Preference Act of 1944, while such people are available. It also lets some current employees in those jobs apply for examination, and the Civil Service Commission may give classified or probational status to those who qualify. A person not entitled to preference can get classified status only under limited conditions, and employees who do not qualify for classification may be replaced from the competitive register.

9739.s: This order makes earlier rules apply to the transportation expenses of civilian officers and employees when departmental functions are returned to the seat of government. It also applies those rules to the transportation of immediate family members and raises the weight limits for household goods and personal effects. For employees transferred before the act was approved, it applies only to those whose positions were transferred after October 11, 1944.

9737.s: This order revokes section 3 of Executive Order 9328 from April 8, 1943. That section had dealt with the authority of the Chairman of the War Manpower Commission in connection with the stabilization of wages, prices, and salaries.

9736.s: This order directs the Director of the Office of Defense Transportation to take possession and control of the transportation system, plants, and facilities of The Monongahela Connecting Railroad Company. It says this is because a labor dispute is interrupting operations and the war effort would be delayed. The Director is to keep transportation service running and may end the takeover when it is no longer needed. The order also says workers may keep their union membership and bargain collectively, as long as their activity does not interfere with operations.

9734.s: This order creates the President's Certificate of Merit, which the President may award to civilians. It is for people who performed a meritorious act or service that aided the United States or another nation fighting in World War II, when no other suitable award exists. The certificate may also be given after death, and no one may receive more than one.

9735.s: This order creates a Cabinet Committee on Palestine and related problems, led by the Secretary of State and made up of the Secretaries of State, War, and the Treasury. It is set up to help the President review recommendations about displaced Jews in Europe and Palestine and decide what steps the United States should take. The committee may propose measures, carry out approved policies and programs, work with other governments and organizations, and use government records, personnel, and travel support when needed.

9733.s: This order directs the Civil Service Commission to certify certain people for probational appointment in Post Office field service jobs. It applies to people whose names were on eligible lists, who entered the armed forces during the stated period, were separated under honorable conditions, and are still qualified for the job, if they ask for restoration or certification within the set time. It also applies to eligibles who qualify under the Veterans' Preference Act and have 10-point preference, for filling vacancies and replacing temporary and war-service appointees.

9732.s: This order changes the name used in an earlier executive order and in related regulations from "Petroleum Conservation Division" to "Oil and Gas Division." It affects the administration and enforcement of the act on interstate and foreign commerce in petroleum and its products produced in violation of state law.

9731.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Hudson & Manhattan Railroad Company and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees may not change the conditions that led to the dispute except by agreement.

9730.s: This order amends a prior executive order on foreign economic functions and surplus property in foreign areas. It says nothing in the order limits the Department of State’s authority to hire personnel or make other spending it sees as necessary to carry out its duties under that part or under the Surplus Property Act of 1944.

9729.s: This order gives the Director of the Office of Defense Transportation authority to allocate the use of transportation equipment and facilities by rail, motor, water, and air carriers when needed in the public interest and for national defense. It also lets the Director obtain information, require reports and records, inspect books and property, investigate, administer oaths, and require witness testimony and evidence. Vessel allocations by the Administrator of the War Shipping Administration must follow cargo requirements and priorities set by the Director. The order does not limit the authority of the Administrator of the Civilian Production Administration under other executive orders.

9727.s: This order takes control of the transportation systems, plants, and facilities of the listed railroads. It directs the Director of the Office of Defense Transportation to run them so rail service stays continuous and uninterrupted. The order also lets railroad management keep operating as much as possible, keeps existing contracts in force unless changed, and says workers may keep union membership and collective bargaining rights subject to the order. It applies to the listed carriers and can also be extended to other rail carriers in the continental United States if needed.

9726.s: This order transfers the fiscal work for lend-lease and reverse lend-lease matters from the Department of State to the Treasury Department. The Treasury Department will handle the accounts, fiscal records, reports, billing, collections, and related recordkeeping for those matters. The Department of State keeps its other duties under the act and must still share related agreements and documents with Treasury.

9728.s: The order authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to take possession of certain bituminous coal mines and operate them, or arrange for their operation, in the interest of the war effort. It also lets the Secretary deal with property and other assets used with the mines, and directs federal agencies to help. The order keeps existing employment terms in place at first, protects workers and people seeking jobs, and recognizes workers' rights to organize, bargain collectively, and take part in concerted activities that do not interfere with mine operations.

9724.s: This order changes the pay rules for the members of the National Wage Stabilization Board. It says public members will get $10,000 a year, and the other members will not get other pay from the United States but will get travel and necessary expenses plus $25 a day for subsistence. It applies to the Board members and takes effect as of December 31, 1945.

9725.s: This order designates the Alien Property Custodian to administer certain powers given to the President under the Trading with the Enemy Act, as amended. It also allows the Custodian to delegate needed tasks to officers and employees of that office. The order does not revoke or limit any power already delegated to the Custodian.

9723.s: This order revokes Executive Order No. 9205 and ends the President's War Relief Control Board. It directs the Secretary of State to liquidate the Board's activities and obligations, wind up its affairs, and use its personnel, property, records, and unspent funds as needed.

9721.s: This order lets certain civilian federal employees be transferred to public international organizations that the United States participates in, if the organization asks and the agency head agrees. It also gives some transferred employees classified civil-service status, and some may be rehired in their former job or one with the same seniority, status, and pay if their service ends without prejudice. The Civil Service Commission may issue rules to carry out the order.

9722.s: This order directs the Secretary of War to reassign the functions, duties, and powers of the service of supply command and the Commanding General, Services of Supply. Those duties are to be moved to other agencies and officers of the War Department as the Secretary of War decides is appropriate.

9720.s: This order discontinues several naval airspace reservations and defensive sea areas. It affects the Sitka and Subic Bay naval airspace reservations and the Subic Bay, Manila Bay, Los Angeles-Long Beach Harbor, San Diego, San Francisco, Columbia River Entrance, and Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound defensive sea areas.

9719.s: This order creates a board of three members to investigate disputes between several air carriers and certain of their employees represented by the Air Line Pilots Association, International. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the carriers and their employees may not change the conditions involved in the disputes except by agreement.

9718.s: This order ends the Petroleum Administration for War and the offices of Petroleum Administrator and Deputy Petroleum Administrator. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to wind up the agency’s affairs using its personnel, records, property, and funds as needed.

9717.s: This order directs the Emergency Board to investigate disputes between the Railway Express Agency, Inc. and certain of its employees represented by the International Association of Machinists and the International Brotherhood of Blacksmiths, Drop Forgers and Helpers. It also adds those disputes to the board’s report to the President. From April 24, 1946 and for thirty days after the board reports, the agency and the employees may not change the conditions out of which the disputes arose except by agreement.

9716.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Railway Express Agency, Inc. and certain of its employees. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the board reports, no change may be made in the conditions that led to the dispute except by agreement.

9715.s: The order directs that the National Flag be displayed at half staff on all public buildings of the United States for thirty days. It also directs that the usual military and naval honors be rendered, and that U.S. embassies, legations, and consulates in foreign countries fly the flag at half staff for thirty days. These directions are in memory of Harlan Fiske Stone, the Chief Justice of the United States.

9714.s: This order changes a prior rule on non-military and non-naval transportation on Army and Navy air transports. It replaces “eighteen months” with “two years” in one section, and it adds a rule that when Army or Navy aircraft are flown on special missions for the exclusive use of other Federal agencies, payment must be based on actual cost. This affects Army and Navy personnel and Federal agencies using those flights on official Government business.

9713.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between the Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railway Company and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, and for thirty days after the report, the company and its employees may not change the conditions behind the dispute except by agreement.

9712.s: This order amends a prior order that extends the classified civil service. It allows some people who left covered jobs to serve in the military or naval forces to be reinstated in their old job or a similar job, if they were honorably discharged, apply within the stated time, and qualify in the required noncompetitive examination.

9711.s: This order covers certain former federal employees and permanent civil-service employees who take civilian jobs with the Military Government authorities in occupied territories. If they are qualified and meet the listed application and certification requirements, they may be reemployed in their original federal job or a similar one with the same seniority, status, and pay. The order also allows some permanent civil-service employees to be transferred there with their consent and the consent of their agency.

9710.s: This order ends the Office of Inter-American Affairs. It transfers certain functions, records, property, funds, and some personnel to the Department of State and the Secretary of State. It also moves the functions tied to several named corporations to the Secretary of State, while ending the rest of the Office’s functions.

9709.s: This order transfers certain U.S. air-navigation, air-traffic-control, airway-communication, and meteorological facilities outside the continental United States to the Department of Commerce when they are no longer needed for military purposes and can help civil aircraft in foreign air commerce. Commerce may make temporary arrangements for the custody, operation, and maintenance of those facilities with foreign governments, international agencies, air carriers, or other suitable private agencies, and may accept funds for services. The order does not apply to loran or other sea and air navigation facilities now operated by the Coast Guard.

9708.s: This order specifies certain communicable diseases for regulations that allow the apprehension, detention, or conditional release of individuals. The purpose is to help prevent the introduction, transmission, or spread of these diseases from foreign countries into the States or possessions, or from one State or possession into another. The diseases listed include anthrax, cholera, diphtheria, gonorrhea, leprosy, plague, smallpox, syphilis, tuberculosis, typhoid fever, typhus, and yellow fever.

9707.s: This order changes a section of an earlier order on consolidating surplus property functions. It keeps certain transferred jobs under the Classification Act and sets pay rules for some positions moved to the War Assets Administration. It also lets the Secretary of War and the Secretary of the Navy temporarily detail military personnel to help carry out the transferred and consolidated functions.

9706.s: This order changes the rules for three military campaign medals. It says the European-African-Middle Eastern Campaign Medal cannot be awarded for service after November 8, 1945, and the American Campaign Medal and Asiatic-Pacific Campaign Medal cannot be awarded for service after March 2, 1946. It also says members and former members of the land and naval forces, including the Women's Reserve of the United States Naval Reserve and former members of the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps, who served in the continental United States for an aggregate period of one year between December 7, 1941, and March 2, 1946, may be awarded the American Campaign Medal under regulations set by the Secretary of War and Secretary of the Navy.

9705.s: This order gives the Economic Stabilization Director the power to give final approval, on the President’s behalf, to orders issued by the Secretary of Agriculture under section 8c of the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937. It also lets the director carry out the President’s functions and authority under that section. The order ratifies and confirms earlier approvals made by the Economic Stabilization Director and the Stabilization Administrator for those agriculture orders.

9704.s: This order gives the American Battle Monuments Commission control over the materials and design of memorial monuments and buildings in American cemeteries outside the United States and its territories and possessions. It also lets the commission make rules and supervise their erection. If a foreign country or political subdivision authorizes it, the commission may also control the materials and design of memorial monuments and buildings there that commemorate American armed forces.

9702.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate a dispute between The Alton Railroad Company, other listed carriers, and certain employees represented by railroad labor organizations. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. During that time, the carriers and their employees may not change the conditions involved in the dispute except by agreement.

9701.s: This order reserves fissionable materials in certain public lands and other lands owned by the United States. It also gives the United States the right to enter those lands and prospect for, mine, and remove those materials. The order revokes an earlier executive order and sets rules for how some released lands may be applied for by qualified World War II veterans, other claimants with valid rights, and later the general public.

9703.s: This order sets rules for medical, surgical, and dental care and hospitalization for certain Coast Guard, Coast and Geodetic Survey, Public Health Service, and former Lighthouse Service personnel. It also covers some dependents of those personnel. The rules say when Service facilities must be used, when outside care may be authorized, and what treatment retired or absent personnel may get.

9700.s: This order creates a three-member board to investigate disputes between the Texas & New Orleans Railroad Company and certain employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. The board must report its findings to the President within thirty days. From the date of the order and for thirty days after the board reports, the railroad company and its employees may make no change in the conditions that led to the disputes except by agreement.

9699.s: This order re-establishes the Office of Economic Stabilization with the same functions, powers, and duties it had before. It transfers the functions, authority, records, property, personnel, and funds of the Office of the Stabilization Administrator to that office. It also re-establishes the Economic Stabilization Board and lists its members, including several Cabinet officials and two representatives each of labor, management, and farmers.

9698.s: This order designates several international organizations as public international organizations under the International Organizations Immunities Act. The Food and Agriculture Organization, the International Labor Organization, the Pan American Union, the United Nations, and the United National Relief and Rehabilitation Administration are covered. It also makes the Department of State the agency that receives applications from other international organizations and sends recommendations to the President.

9697.s: This order directs federal departments and agencies to use their powers to help keep the economy stable during the emergency. It tells the Price Administrator to adjust price ceilings in some hardship cases, and it sets rules for wage or salary increases that may be approved by wage stabilization agencies. It also says arbitration awards and public fact-finding recommendations on wages must follow these standards.

9694.s: This order says certain income, excess-profits, and declared value excess-profits tax returns for 1939 and later years must be open to inspection by the War Contracts Price Adjustment Board. The inspection is subject to conditions in a Treasury decision approved the same day. It also directs that the order be published in the Federal Register.

9692.s: This order amends a prior order on Merchant Marine awards. It authorizes the Administrator to issue a Merchant Marine Honorable Service Button as proof of honorable service to a person who receives a certificate of substantially continuous service. It also says the design of the plaques, medal, ribbons, and service button may not duplicate awards from the War Department, Navy Department, or Coast and Geodetic Survey.

9691.s: This order directs the Civil Service Commission to resume open competitive examinations and register eligible applicants for permanent federal jobs in the classified civil service. It also lets the Commission set temporary rules during the transition, use special examiner boards and committees, and require agencies to follow veterans' preference rules.
